Explain.

This bill is similar to the one which I introduced last year at the end of the session but which could not be discussed at that time. Its purpose is to amend the form of the oath of allegiance which all public officials have to take. It is intended to change the word "possessions" to "dominions," to agree with the title which His Majesty has had since the Imperial conference of 1926. speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised the hon.
member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) that at an early date I would endeavour to make a statement with respect to the wheat agreement. As the provincial legislation in connection with this matter will be introduced to-day or to-morrow I think it desirable to make a statement at this time. During the last few months the dominion government and the governments of the three prairie provinces have been Considering the action which should be taken to make effective the London wheat agreement so far as it relates to Canadian interests. Legislation has been agreed upon by the four governments and will be introduced to-day or to-morrow in the legislatures of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The proposed legislation empowers the lieutenant governor in council in each of the provinces to set up what is termed an emergency wheat control board, with power to licence and restrict within the province sales and deliveries of wheat. Provision is made also that in addition to or in lieu of such board a joint board may be established by the three prairie provinces or by one or more or all of the provinces in conjunction with the dominion. Such a board, if created, will be clothed with all the powers usually vested in what is commonly described as a "wheat board." The provisions dealing with the
Wheat Agreement-Mr. Bennett

licensing of sales and deliveries of wheat within the several provinces can, of course, be enacted by the legislature of a province, but legislation of this parliament is required to permit control of sales and deliveries outside the provinces. With respect to a wheat board, parliament will be invited to enact the necessary legislation to enable the government, in the event of the four governments being of the opinion that the necessity for same exists, to cooperate with the provinces in establishing a board, with all the necessary authority and powers to deal with any situation which may arise. It will be observed that the proposal contemplates the enactment of enabling legislation so that problems that may arise by reason of an unexpectedly large crop or from any other circumstance can be effectively dealt with.
The bills introduced to-day or to-morrow- I believe it is possible that they may not all be introduced to-day-into the legislatures of the several provinces will provide that the lieutenant governor in council shall, on and after the date upon which the act founded on the bill is assented to, and prior to the date of the establishment of the board or joint board, as therein provided, have power by order in council to make all such orders, rules and regulations, and do all such acts and things as in the opinion of the lieutenant governor in council may be necessary and requisite to bring the production of wheat in the province concerned in the year 1934 into proper alignment with the estimated current export demand for the crop season 1934-36 and normal domestic requirements in the same period, having regard to the quota applicable to the Dominion of Canada as provided. by article 2 of the London wheat agreement.
I may add, for the information of the house, that officials of this government have been in the past few weeks in consultation with the governments of the three prairie provinces. The steps already taken, together with the contemplated action, as provided by the proposed legislation, will, in the opinion of the governments concerned, fully implement the undertakings of the dominion under the London agreement..
Some time ago the hon. member for Wey-burn asked a question which I promised I would answer more full}'' when I had obtained further information which I was then securing. Hon. members will recall that negotiations and consultations among the four overseas wheat exporting countries had been in progress under the auspices of the League of Nations for some time before the London w'heat agreement was signed. As a result of

those discussions it was possible to allocate among the overseas exporting countries quotas for the crop year 1933-34 within the terms of article 1 of the agreement. At the time of the signing of the agreement, no quota had been agreed upon for the U.S.S.R., nor had a final agreement with respect to such quota yet been concluded but it is expected that at the meeting at Rome next month a satisfactory arrangement will be reached.
The four overseas exporting countries agreed, by article 2 of the London agreement:
to limit their exports of wheat during the crop year the 1st August, 1934, to the 31st July, 1935, to maximum figures 15 per cent less in the case of each country than the average out-turn on the average acreage sown during the period 1931-33 inclusive after deducting normal domestic requirements.
The determining of the quotas under the provisions of this article is, in the main, a statistical operation. In the case of the four overseas exporting countries, the three years 1931, 1932 and 1933, are used for computing the average acreage, and the yield per acre is determined over a ten-year period.
It is to be borne in mind that the purpose of the agreement is to raise the price of wheat, which can only be done when the surplus carryovers have been removed from the market. In this regard we must distinguish between formal obligations contained in an international agreement and collateral measures of domestic policy which may have to be taken to give effect to the provisions of the agreement. The measures of domestic policy taken by the signatory countries will not be identical. Argentina and Australia have, for instance, stated that they are not in a position to agree to any precise acreage reduction although they are willing to reduce their exports by the accepted figures and to take the necessary action to prevent the accumulation of further surplus stocks. The United States has definitely decided to reduce acreage by 15 per cent and has put into effect a wheat adjustment program for that purpose.
So far as Canada is concerned, having accepted an export quota for the period ending 31st July, 1935, it becomes a matter of national interest that our production in that period should not exceed the domestic requirements plus the export demand. The measures necessary to ensure this have been determined by the appropriate Canadian authorities. It is obvious, of course, that there is no international agreement determining the methods to be adopted by the governments of Canada and the several provinces to give effect to the agreement.

Wheat Agreement-Mr. Bennett
It might be well to refer to a statement made in this house as to the influence of government purchases of wheat in recent years in increasing normal carryovers. The use of the words " government purchases " is, of course, inaccurate, for what the government has done is to guarantee the obligations created by the purchasing agency, namely, the
pool agency at Winnipeg. The following table gives the Food Research Institute figures for world carryovers for the past six years, as of August 1, together with the Canadian carryovers on the same dates, and the 'Percentages which the Canadian stocks form of the world totals:

Owing to the abnormal crop of 1932 the world carryover in 1933 had reached 1,106 million bushels, the Canadian carryover being 219 million bushels or 19-8 .per cent of the whole.
Most of .the increase in world carryovers of wheat has been due to the inability to absorb the huge wheat crops of 1928 and 1932. The record world crop of 1928, which amounted to 4,712 million bushels or to 3,905 million bushels-ex Russia-caused the major rise of 265 million bushels between August 1, 1928, and August 1, 1929. There was then no great increase in carryovers until the large crop of 1932 caused ani increase of 110 million bushels between August 1, 1932, and August 1, 1933. There will be a decrease on August 1, 1934.
Canada was carrying 13 per cent of the world's supply on August 1, 1928. It increased to 13-8 per cent by August, 1930. It remained at the 1930 level throughout 1931 and 1932. From 1928 until 1932 there was only a fractional variation in that five-year period. That ratio was not disturbed until August last, when it reached 19-8 per cent. We need not search far to discover the cause of the increase. The crop of 1932 in this country reached the huge .total of 443,000,000 bushels from a record of 27,200,000 acres. Our exports from that crop reached the very large total of 264,000,000 bushels, or 43 per cent of the total export trade of the world for that year, as compared with the ten-year average of 37 per cent. I particularly direct the attention of the house to these figures. There can surely be no complaint when our share of the world available trade reached such large proportions, and yet, in spite of such unusually large exports in that year, there was left
from .that crop some 80,000,000 bushels to be added to our carryovers from past years, dating back to 1928.
Prices have not been maintained at a fixed level but rather they were supported, particularly during the seasons of the year when farmers were, from necessity, forced sellers of their production in order to meet the demands and needs of their creditors. Export demand, at such times, was utterly inadequate to absorb the farmers' sales, as it always had been throughout past years, and owing to world excessive supplies, speculative as well as investment buyers, who in normal times were purchasers of wheat, were practically non-existent. Under these circumstances, the government has enabled the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, to purchase all grain that was not otherwise- sold. Had it not done so, what would have been the position of the wheat market to-day? The farmer would have hauled his grain to the elevator, would have been unable to sell it and there it would have remained and finally would have been baoked up on to his farm; and you would have had absolute chaos, which would have been destructive .to the whole economic life of Canada. There has been no speculation in wheat, and the wheat that has been .bought is now being held and sold as demand offers, not for speculation but for export. It would therefore appear that any criticisms that the action of the government in preventing chaotic marketing conditions has brought about an increased surplus are not founded on facts.
The London agreement sets the world quota of wheat exports in the 1933-34 crop year at

As the table shows, 26,000,000 bushels of this had been shipped to the end of February and there remains a balance of 18,000,000 bushels.
The advisory committee set up under the provisions of the London agreement is holding a meeting at Rome on April 5 next, when the matter of increasing the consumption of wheat will be discussed by the countries affected and such measures taken as, in the opinion of those present, will result in the diminution of the surplus carryovers that threaten the wheat prices of the world.
The question of endeavouring to settle the final quota for Russia will also be brought before the advisory committee and, if possible, disposed of.

The Prime Minister says that Canada's quota under the agreement would be 200,000,000 bushels, but if we figure our quota on the basis suggested by himself, that is a three-year average acreage and a ten-year average yield, our quota would be 292,000,000 bushels. Will he explain the discrepancy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman was unable to follow me because I was reading rather rapidly. The quota for the year ending July 31, 1935, is to be settled in the manner I have indicated by the statisticians on the three-year average acreage multiplied by the ten-year average yield. The quota of 200,000,000 bushels for the crop year ending July 31, 1934, was settled by agreement on the basis of the figures supplied as to our crop, and the figures I have just given as to the shipments already made and the balances remaining to be made indicate that the quantity -was perhaps in excess of any amount that we would be able to ship.

I am not yet clear as to the meaning of this agreement. If I understood the Prime Minister aright, our quota for the year 1934-35 is to be based upon the ten-year average yield on a three-year average acreage, but article 2 of the agreement says the three-year average yield on a three-year average acreage. That is the difficulty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at the agreement, that is not what it says. I admit that it is open to that construction, but if he will look at it carefully I think he will see that it does not say that. It says 15 per cent less in the case of each country than the average out-turn on the average acreage sown during the period, and the average out-turn is for ten years and not for three.
The ten-year period is not mentioned at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, but that is the fact.
It is not in the agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is how the statisticians agreed that the quota should be reached. That is, the average yield was taken over a period of ten years as being fair. I think the figure is 174 bushels per acre, but it was thought a fair average acreage would be one taken over a three-year period.
Are all the other countries agreeable to that interpretation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; that was the agreement arrived at, and when the agreement was drafted late at night there was some difficulty about the translation. That was observed, but there was no difference as to the manner in which the computation was to be made. There was difficulty in determining what, under those circumstances, should be the quota for Russia, and I have explained that point. This talk about a supplementary agree-

Translations Bureau-Mr. Chevrier
ment is talk that relates to the quota for Russia, and when that quota has been determined the whole matter will then be reduced to a formal document. In the meantime, as I explained to the hon. gentleman, we agreed to 200,000,000 bushels as the quota for Canada for the year ending July 31, 1934. The manner of the computation for 1934-35 is as I have indicated: a three-year average acreage multiplied by the average yield over a ten-year period.

I desire to ask a question of the Secretary of State (Mr. 'Cahan). Perhaps I should have asked this question in French but as I had no opportunity of communicating the matter to him beforehand, I think I should in order to be fair ask the question in English. I desire to refer the hon. minister to page 1282 of Hansard, about the middle of the page, where he is reported as having said:
I have received statements from certain gentlemen who have qualifications as translators and who are bilingual by education and experience.
On the next page, on the lefthand side, in answer to a question which I asked, the hon. minister was pleased to answer:
You will have to seek the information from them.
Now I have before me the file of the daily French paper, La Presse of Montreal, of Friday, March 9, in which the parliamentary
correspondent of that paper has placed the following words in the mouth of the hon. minister. In order to do no injustice to the minister I shall not endeavour to translate his speech into current English, but so that there may be no mistake about the accuracy of the translation I shall do it literally:
The worth of this work having been put in doubt, and not having myself unfortunately that which is necessary to judge of these criticisms. I have addressed myself to two recognized authorities: Pierre Lefort special correspondent of La Presse, and the Chanoine Chartiem, vice rector of the university of Montreal.
The two questions which I now desire to direct to the hon. minister are, which of the two reports, that of Hansard or this press report, correctly reports what the hon. minister said at that moment? Did the hon. minister in any manner solicit any opinion from these two experts, as is alleged by Pierre Lefort in this article?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

As a minister of the crown I think that if I wish to know whether a translation made by a translator of this house is correct or not I have a perfect right to ask the opinion of any gentleman I choose.

Then I shall summon
these people and find out from them.

Fisheries-to assist in the conservation and development of the deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $85,000.
I think it is in order to ask the minister what I asked yesterday on the same estimate, as to the intention of the government or the department in regard to Hudson bay and James bay.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I listened yesterday with great attention to my hon. friend in regard to the possibilities for the fishing industry in Hudson bay and James bay. I have discussed the matter with my officials and I must state frankly that we cannot contemplate any further investigation in those bays this year. It may be that in the future we can do something, but not this year. I may state to my hon. friend for his information that private interests are extensively concerned in the fishing industry in those waters.

As a matter of fact, we are helping as much as possible all those who desire to enter the fishing industry there. In 1931 we issued three fishing permits; in 1932 four other permits for fishing in those bays, in 1933 we issued four permits, and this year we have issued one permit to the Albany River Fishing Company, Limited. We anticipate that many other companies will start fishing next summer. The department is quite satisfied that surveys have been made, are being made and will be made during the coming season by those private concerns in order to locate the best spots for fishing in those waters.

Will the minister tell the committee if those private concerns have any direction from the government to make those inquiries? As the minister appreciates, my question relates to an expanse of water of nearly 700,000 square miles, so unless those private concerns go there with definite direction from the government they are not likely to make an investigation for the sake of the government. I appreciate what the minister has said, but will he be a little more explicit as to when we might expect a more thorough inquiry to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The report of the
investigation made in 1930 might be of some use to those interested, and I may add that a few days ago I had a request from a certain individual who wants permits for several fishing boats. That gentleman told me that he knew the best spots for fishing in those two. bays, and that other people also knew where to go. So at the moment I do not think it would be advisable for the government to incur the expense of a further survey. If in future we have such requests from various parties we will look into the matter and see if we would be justified in making a further survey.

I may tell the minister that the request comes from that entire section of the country, and surely the pressure should be as great coming from the people living in that country as it would be coming from people directly interested in the fidhing. I believe the government owes it to itse'lf and to our section of the country to take the lead in such an investigation and not leave it to private interests. I think they should take the initiative, and I believe the work should be wholly under the direction of the government.

I should
like to ask my hon. friend if it is not true that in 1930 the then Minister of Fisheries

Supply-Fisheries-C onservation
did have an investigation made into the possibilities of commercial fishing in Hudson bay, and that the report was adverse?
The report was adverse, but the investigation took only a short time.

I should like to ask the minister if he has any report to give the committee with reference to the negotiations that were supposed to be going on between his department and the government of Quebec with regard to increased cooperation between the provincial and federal governments. I remember that a long debate took place in this house two or three years ago, and the then Minister of Fisheries, who is now Minister of Finance, said there would be cooperation as far as this government could bring it about between the federal and provincial governments. I saw in the press some time after that some mention of interviews between the minister who is piloting these estimates today and officials of the provincial government with the view of improving conditions in Quebec. I should like to ask the minister if he has any report to give tthe committee as to the progress that has been made along these lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have no report to
make on the subject as yet. It is true that conferences and interviews took place and that correspondence has been exchanged between the provincial and federal authorities with regard to cooperation having in view the betterment of fisheries in Quebec, but nothing definite has been arrived at as yet. We had planned a French school for fishermen and inspectors on the Gaspe coast, in Gaspe itself. I hope these negotiations will eventually lead to the establishment of such a school, where two or three French teachers will instruct in the curing and canning of fish and so on, but nothing definite has been agreed upon. The provincial government was supposed to supply the building and the federal authorities were to provide the teachers.

During the last few days I have been in receipt of many resolutions from various municipalities in the province of Quebec, who apparently are alarmed because the government has not made the headway that was expected. I have none of the resolutions before me, but I think I received about a half dozen to-day, and they all complain of the situation which exists in the fishing industry in the province of Quebec. Some of them even go so far as to ask that the order in council passed in 1922 giving the administration of fisheries to the provincial
government should be repealed, if that is the only way to bring about an improvement in the condition, and I think I even went so far as .to advocate such a step during the course of the debate in this house two or three years ago. In view of the difficulties with which we are faced to-day, and in view of the fact that a moment ago the minister said that it was hoped to do something on the coast of Gaspe, though apparently nothing has been done yet, I think this is the proper time to have the minister who is in charge of this very important department make a statement not only as to what is supposed to have been done but as to something tangible that will be done in order to relieve the situation. It is all very well for the minister to come here year after year and tell us that negotiations have been entered into between his government and the provincial government, but nothing has been done, and the people on the north shore are asking that action be taken by this government.
I do not think the minister can get away with that answer to-day. Last year we were told that an institution would be established on the coast of Gaspe to help the fishermen in the province of Quebec. I think at that time the minister said he could not proceed with the project because of the lack of money, that they were not ready to undertake this work. This year I think some steps should be taken in that direction, because if this is not done the fishing industry will go from bad to worse. The people in that part of the country have had a hard time to make both ends meet; they have been barely able to secure a living for their families and themselves, and most of the fishermen in the part of the country which I have the honour to represent are on direct relief. I have no doubt the minister has recevied many requests that these people be assisted. I think we should be given a better statement than the minister has given so far; I do not think it is enough to say that this project could not be proceeded with. Why has nothing been done? Why can they get nothing done for the fishermen of the province of Quebec, when a resolution was adopted by this house two years ago urging this government to cooperate with the government of that province? That resolution was tantamount to an order directing the government to take some steps in that direction. What steps have been taken, and in what way? To-day the minister is mum; he has nothing to say as to what is going to be done, if anything. If we cannot get ministers of the crown more responsive

Supply-Fisheries-Conservation
to the people than .those we now have sitting on the treasury benches, some day the people will clear out the whole administration. I am surprised that the minister is not able to give me any answer.
Give him a chance.

I am going to give him a chance. I ask him to give me the reason why this school has not been started in Gaspe, which was supposed to be the first step. The minister need not tell me there is no money; there is money for some other institutions, some other boards and for other ventures which here and there the government have seen fit to patronize. Surely there ought to be a certain amount of money to put at the disposal of the Department of Fisheries for the help of the fishermen of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, may' I add a few words to what has been stated by the hon. member for Charlevoix Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain). It cannot be gainsaid that the situation of fishermen on the Gaspe coast and of those on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river is absolutely intolerable. However, we must take into consideration the fact that in 1922 the Liberal government, passed an order in council transferring all its fishery rights to the government of Quebec. Since that date, the fisheries come directly under the administration of the provincial government. It is now requested that the Dominion government collaborate with the Quebec government, and it is contended that if there is no co-operation or if anything goes wrong, the Dominion government will be held responsible; but when all is well the Quebec government gets the credit for it. There is but one remedy and that is to cancel the 1922 order in council.
I suggested and requested it.

What should be done is the return of the control of all the Quebec fisheries to the Dominion government and to put matters as they stood before this order in council was passed. Were we to probe this question, or hold an inquiry in order to find out why the control of the Quebec fisheries was taken away from the Dominion government, it would be shown that it was simply to favour a few persons who wanted to take possession of the salmon fishing in the rivers on the north shore and the Gaspe coast.
Name these persons.

The list would be too long; the hon. member for Laprairie Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) must be aware of this fact because he has had the occasion of visiting Gaspe and the north shore. These persons intended not only to take possession of the salmon rivers of the Gaspe peninsula and the north shore of the St. Lawrence, but to also control the estuaries of these rivers and that was the reason the dominion government was requested, in 1922, to pass an order in council. I think that the only real remedy to the situation, under the circumstances, as I had the occasion of suggesting to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) would be to cancel the order in council of 1922, so that the control of the fisheries of Quebec would be returned to the dominion government as it was previously and as it is the case in all other provinces.

I do not agree with all the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec Montmorency (Mr. Dorion), for instance, when he states: when all is well the government of the province of Quebec takes the credit, and when all goes wrong, the Dominion government is blamed.
All are aware that if depression exists in this country, the dominion government must be held responsible. It is not the provincial government which is at the helm of affairs in Ottawa, but those who sit to your right, sir. The fisheries are federal property and only their administration is the prerogative of the provincial government.
As to the repeal of the order in council of 1922, I suggested it, when I brought up the subject about two years ago and a discussion ensued. I again suggest it, to-day, because the Quebec government has not at its disposal experts like the dominion officials of the Department of Marine. The order in council not having been repealed, we are forced to request the co-operation and good will of the two governments. The hon. minister cannot assert that Quebec refused to cooperate in improving the fisheries of the province. He cannot make such a statement, because it would not be true. The Quebec government is willing to co-operate with the Ottawa government-whether it is a Liberal or Conservative administration-to improve the situation. Negotiations have been carried on to this effect. I should like to know why, after stating, I think, last year, that a biological station would be established on the Gaspe coast as soon as possible, the minister did not implement this promise of establishing that station to help the fisheries of Gaspe and those of the north shore of the St. Law-

Supply-Fisheries-Conservation
rence river. Why this delay to open up this biological station? The establishment of this station with the co-operation of the hon. minister and his officials together with that of the Quebec department of Fisheries, would be an embryo, a first help, on the part of both governments, to improve the situation of the fisheries on the Gaspe coast and the north shore of the St. Lawrence river.
We agree on that point: we must endeavour to improve the situation of the fisheries, however to reach this aim, the dominion government and the hon. Minister of Marine must show their good will and put in practise what they advocated. We are informed that the dominion government could not do more because apparently no funds were at their disposal. The government seem to have funds for many enterprises; however, when it is a question of the Quebec fisheries, there seems to be very little funds. I think the government could find the necessary funds to establish this biological station and the Quebec government would certainly contribute its quota.
Mr. Chairman-
Is there no reply?

Referring to page 606 of Hamsard, I find that the fish exports to the various parts of the British Empire, in 1933, that is, after the Imperial Conference, amounted to $2,116,116 less than in 1930, and to foreign countries, $9,521,337 less; a total decrease, comparing 1938 to 1930, of $11,637,453. Therefore, the Canadian fish exports to the various parts of the British Empire and foreign countries have considerably decreased.
Would the hon. member kindly give the amount in pounds instead of money?

My reply to the hon. member is that I put the same question to the Bureau of Statistics and I could not obtain the amount in pounds. The answer would have been too long because the quantity of each species of fish would have had to be enumerated. If the hon. member wishes to get the information he may forward his request to the hon. Minister of Marine who, he will find, is always willing, courteous and an example for the hon. member to emulate in the house. As to fish and fishery products, by comparing 1932 to 1930, we note a decrease of $21,847,107. May I ask the Minister of Marine why this decrease in value in the
fishery products and how many fishermen were affected by this situation?
Mr. Chairman-

I shall avail myself of this opportunity-without wishing to interrupt the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil)-to point out an error in Hansard on the same page, in a quotation by the right hon. Prime Minister. In the second column 188 cwts. of fish is mentioned, while it should read 188,000 cwts.

Mr. Chairman, this question of cooperation between the two governments of Ottawa and Quebec in connection with the fisheries, dates away back. I had the privilege, in 1897, of being the Liberal candidate, in Gaspe, against the Hon. Mr. Flynn, then Prime Minister of Quebec, His campaign plank was the fishery question, he maintained that the fisheries should be the prerogative of the Quebec government. He won his election by a majority of one vote-that was rather a small majority. Eleven votes which he gained following a recount, were the result of a cablegram from London, which he received a few days before the voting day, informing him of the Privy Council's decision, that in the future salmon fishing permits would be issued by the Quebec government. So they have been issued for quite a long time. Therefore, if we go back to 1897, almost ancient history, thirty-five years ago, we note that, at that period, there already existed a divergency of views between the two governments.
It gave me much pleasure, to hear from the lips of the minister, on Friday, that he was, at present, negotiating with the Quebec government in order to come to some arrangement in this respect. What interests me most, is the welfare of the people. These poor fishermen, on behalf of wbom Mgr. Ross, the eminent bishop of Gaspe, has pleaded, are very downcast, at present, and an "entente" between the two governments is greatly hoped for. I am pleased to hear that the hon. Minister of Fisheries is considering the question, and I have the assurance that the Hon. Mr. Laferte, Minister of Fisheries, in Quebec, is also disposed to do everything possible to arrive at some arrangement. If it is necessary, for the welfare of the fisherman and the success of the Quebec fisheries, that the provincial government should release the control which it has over the fisheries, at present; I feel certain that the Quebec prime minister, who is broadminded and highly esteemed in the province would take such a



Supply-Fisheries-Conservation
step. Proofs would have to be given him first-and that is but fair-that the Quebec government is not in a position to look after the fisheries in deep water. On the south shore of the Baie des Chaleurs, the fisheries are owned by the province of New Brunswick. This province allows the Dominion government to administer its fisheries. Such an arrangement might be possible between the Quebec provincial government and the Dominion government.
I was pleased to hear the hon. Minister of Fisheries state, last Friday, that, while on his visits to the GaspS peninsula he had had a talk with Bishop Ross, and had himself ascertained that Quebec fisheries were, indeed, in a sad plight. I trust that before long some "modus vivendi" will be agreed upon between the two governments and a considerable improvement will be the result.
Meantime, I congratulate the minister on his intention of establishing a biological school at Gaspe or in the best suited locality the commission may find in that county, thus giving these people whose forbears were the first to settle this country, instructors speaking the French language. We too often forget, we, French Canadian members, who constantly speak English in deference to our colleagues, that both languages are official. When the Dominion government places English speaking instructors in New Brunswick, the people of Quebec are likewise entitled to have French speaking instructors- I was, therefore, pleased to hear that the minister intended to place French speaking instructors in this new biological school which will cater not only to the counties of Gaspe, Bonaven-ture and the Magdalen Islands, but also to the whole gulf of St. Lawrence, including the counties of Saguenay and Chicoutimi; thus putting us on an equal footing with the people >f other provinces. We have to contend with our climate and strive against difficulties which exist neither in British Columbia nor in Nova Scotia where the fisheries are opened twelve months in the year. For these reasons, I think the Minister of Fisheries and the Dominion government should see that the people of Gaspe receive the necessary help, even a generous one. Owing to the difficulties encountered in earning a livelihood, the population of my county, I regret to state, has dropped by a few thousands within the last 25 years, due to the lack of encouragement, communication facilities, markets to dispose of their fish and other reasons for which no government in particular is responsible, neither provincial nor federal.
[Mr. Marcil.3
Indeed, this problem must be solved and if the hon. minister can come to some arrangement with the Quebec government in order to settle this question, he will be looked upon as the benefactor of those people.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first, in reply to the question of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr Pouliot) who has noted a decrease in the exportation of the fishery products, I may state, that in no way is this astonishing, ii we consider that, owing to the world-wide crisis, which has lasted three or four years, all countries are exporting less products. The lower price obtained is also one of the causes of the decrease in exports.
I can only state to my hon. friend that the Department of Fisheries is doing its utmost to foster the exportation of our sea and river products, by making regulations and seeing that they are enforced, so that our products may be shipped abroad in the best condition possible, endeavouring thereby, to raise the standard of our products on foreign markets. I feel certain that within a few years our fish exports will greatly increase.
I am somewhat amazed to hear the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain) criticize so sharply the Quebec provincial administration of fisheries.

I did not
criticize it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In 1922, however, our Quebec government friends requested the administration of the provincial fisheries-
I was not consulted in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -under the plea that the provincial government was in a better position to put that administration on a more productive basis, and improve the lot of the fishermen of that province.

Especially
the salmon fishermen.

consulted concerning the matter.

-and
the arrangement which was made between the.* provincial and Dominion governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

No, pardon. If the hon. minister will allow me, I did not represent, at the time, the Saguenay county, my constituency only extended to the Saguenay river, I did not represent the northern coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My
hon. friend had his eyes on the whole northern coast then, and must have taken an interest in the welfare of the fishermen.
I was not as well acquainted with the situation of the fishermen as I am to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It was precisely because he was interested in the welfare of the fishermen of that section of the province that he was called upon later, to represent them.
A tout pecheur misericorde.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I must state to my hon. friend that opinions vary among members opposite and the people of Quebec as regards measures to be taken to improve the lot of the Quebec fishermen. Some say: "We shall request this French speaking school at Gaspe." Others say: "That is unnecessary, that is not what we want. What is required is some agreement between the two governments to cancel the 1922 order in council and return the administration of the fisheries to Dominion government." Others again contend: " The Quebec government's administration of the fisheries is above reproach." And I think an attempt was made to prove that the provincial government's administration of the fisheries was efficient, if I am to judge by the debate which took place recently in the Quebec Legislative Assembly. Naturally, a request was made for the collaboration of the Dominion government, however, it was stated: "The province had well looked after the fisheries, improved the lot of the fishermen." I am therefore amazed to-day to hear the hon. member
74726-91j
for Charlevoix-Saguenay draw such a gloomy description of the situation. The hon. member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil) and the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay differ in opinion in this respect. At all events, sir-

Action,
is all I request.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
At present, the fisheries are within the purview of the provincial authorities, and I do not think that one is justified in criticizing the Dominion government in this respect. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay states that he would be willing to request the repeal of the 1922 order in council. Does my hon. friend imagine that we could proceed "ex parte" in this affair? It is an agreement concluded between the Dominion and provincial governments and he knows that it is not by another agreement that we could improve the situation. The Quebec government has never requested us to abrogate what was done in 1922.
. Did my hon. friend suggest to the provincial authorities that they should request the Dominion government to resume the administration of all the fisheries which were under its control ? As to the Acting Minister of Fisheries, he is as willing as he was last year, he has not altered his stand in this respect, he is ready to cooperate and grant all that was requested by the Hon. Mr. Laferte, namely, instructors speaking the French language-

hear 1

-in a school of biology which will be located in Gaspe, on premises chosen by the provincial government. These instructors should even be chosen by the provincial authorities. Young men having a fair knowledge of fisheries were to be assigned to the biological school at Halifax, for a year, so as to acquire a more thorough knowledge of fisheries, thus qualifying them to take charge of the Gaspe school, the following year. I am informed that the Quebec government sent a few young men to Europe to qualify as specialists in fisheries and biology and they are probably those who will take charge of the school referred to. My hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay will realize that one cannot accomplish in one day what we, the Dominion government, intend to carry out in conjunction with the provincial department of fisheries.

Mr. DURANLEAU (Translation) No request of that nature was made to my department by the provincial authorities, likewise none was made by the Dominion government to the provincial government.
I wish to put a question to the hon. minister: What is the yearly catch of fish in each province?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I wish to inform my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) that the Quebec yearly fishery products amounted, in 1928, to $2,976,000; in 1929, to 2,933,000; in 1930, to 12,502,000; in 1931, to $1,952,000, and in 1932, to $1,815,000.

The crisis.

Are the fish
affected by the crisis?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In the prices, yes.

Has the
minister any statistics in connection with the the consumption of fish in the Dominion and what is the total amount of fish exported yearly?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The whole consumption in Canada is about 95 million pounds of fresh, frozen and mildly cured fish.
I want to know what the whole production amounts to-the amount of fish exported and the principal countries importing Canadian fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend will find in the Fisheries statistics for Canada for 1932, the last volume we have, at page 204 and following pages, the list of all countries importing Canadian fish, the kinds of fish, quantities, price and so on. He will see that our best customer is the United States, then the West Indies; South American countries also import from Canada. There is a large list of countries importing Canadian fish.

How much of this $85,000 is to be used for advertising to promote the consumption of fish in Canada? The item is intended for the conservation and development of deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish.
I presume the expression "to assist the demand for fish" means advertising fish to create a demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
We advertise in
various ways in regard to fish. For instance, we have sent to different exhibitions electrical exhibits of all the fish produced by our fisheries. In Toronto at the last exhibition large crowds were attracted by our exhibit, and a few weeks ago a departmental exhibit which did not cost very much was staged in Montreal and proved a great advertisement for our fisheries. I see from the details of this item that we are expending $15,000 to extend the demand for fish.
In what manner will that be expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Apart from the exhibitions we have tried to increase the home demand for fish by employing, as I informed the committee yesterday, Mrs. Spencer who is an outstanding expert in the use of fish for meals. She has attracted crowds all over Canada.
She or the fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Mrs. Spencer with her way of cooking fish. In Montreal and other centres where the French population is large, we have the services of a bilingual lady who cooperates with Mrs. Spencer. They have visited all the convents in the vicinity and have done splendid work with the educators and pupils in those institutions. At the present time we have about six hundred ladies at each demonstration at Eaton's store in Montreal listening to Mrs. Spencer's lectures on the subject of fish.

We all agree that Mrs. Spencer has rendered excellent service to the fish industry of this country, and I hope the department will retain her in her present position. But I understand strong representations were made to the department by the fishing industry through the Canadian Fisheries Association for an appropriation to be made for the purpose of newspaper and magazine advertising in this country in order to create a greater demand in the Canadian market for the products of the industry. I am a little disappointed that no item appears in the estimate for that purpose. I thought

a sufficient amount or part of the $85,000 might be used in that way. I understand only some $46,000 of the $85,000 that was voted last year, was expended. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, prior to Decem-mer 31.

Then it is fair to suppose that the same amount will be used this year. Why cannot the balance be used for advertising purposes, because this money could not be expended in any better way? As hon. members know, the fisheries of the maritime provinces are at the present time in bad shape. The fishermen there, owing to the state of the markets for their products, have been unable to make both ends meet in the last three or four years. The foreign markets have been in very bad shape during the last four or five years, and we have had to depend a great deal on our home market. If we can increase the consumption of fish in our own markets this will help our fishermen more than anything else. The only way in which that can be done is to get our people to eat more fish, and the only way to do that is to advertise, to keep the matter of fish before our people all the time. I believe last year the minister appropriated $85,000 and expended $41,000. Perhaps he could see his way clear to use $40,000 for advertising.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
During the fiscal
year 1932-33 we expended practically the full amount voted, that is, $84,766, but I said just now to my hon. friend that during the present fiscal year, 1933-34, prior to December 31, 1933, on that appropriation of $85,000 we had expended the sum of $46,411. To the last day of February we had expended about $50,000.

Possibly a sufficient amount
might be placed in the supplementary estimates for this purpose. I am sure the minister will agree with me that the money could not be spent in a better way. That will create a demand for fish. It will be remembered that two years ago the department spent some $20,000 for advertising, being assisted by the trade which raised about fifty per cent more, making the total amount some $30,000. Splendid results accrued from this advertising. Nothing has been done recently in the way of advertising except by individual firms and they are not at present in a position to spend any money for advertising, because I do not think there is in Nova Scotia a single firm in the fish business that has broken even in the last three or four years. I believe the time is now opportune for the
government to step in and give all assistance possible to this industry. I would strongly recommend to the minister that he try to have a sufficient amount placed in the supplementary estimates if he cannot take it from this item of $85,000 which appears in the main estimates. I hope he will give the matter his serious consideration.

As the hon. member for
Digby-Annapolis has exhibited a very proper interest in this appropriation, it might be as well to put the details on Hansard because they will reveal possibly something more than the particular information for which he was asking. They will reveal the fact that practically the whole of this $84,766.31 has been spent in the maritime provinces. Where does British Columbia come in, which has furnished the greater part of the fish trade of Canada? According to the Auditor General's report for the year ended March 31, 1933, the amount expended under the heading " Aids in expanding demands for fish " was $13,706.06. There is an item for Mrs. Spencer, who did not come to the coast last year. An amount of $1,200 is included for broadcasting weather reports. Then there is:
Bait collection service-Canso, $1,278.
Canso, so far as I know, is not in British Columbia.
Bait freezers-Canso: salt and ice, $403.25.
Then:
Marie Joseph, painting, $101.32.
Marie Joseph, whoever he or she was, got $101.32 for painting. Whether Marie painted the freezers or a sea picture in oils I do not know. On educational work, wholly in the maritimes, $10,229 was spent. Exhibitions, Lunenburg-I seem to have heard that name somewhere-cost only $4,182. Then we get the big figures; lobster collection service, subsidy to some company, $21,375. Lobster patrol service, a separate item, $21,340. Then a scallop investigation;-we do not raise scallops in British Columbia,-$5,885. Packet service; I do not know what that is, I will ask the minister to tell us that, a subsidy for the steamship Petite, $1,500. I notice that while this Auditor General's report is for the year ended March 31, 1933, the order in council authorizing that was passed April 4, 1933, alter the olose of the fiscal year. Apparently it was some unusual and out of the way expenditure or it would not have had to be covered by a special order in council.
Then, grant to assist in the publication and distribution of the Canadian Fisheries Manual, $2,000. I do not think even the members in British Columbia get a copy of that. And

Supply-Fisheries-Conservation
there is $2,764 for odd items. As far as I know, unless we shared in that small item of the king's printer, practically the whole of that $84,000 was spent in the maritimes. I do not wonder the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) blushes; he might well do so-
I do not feel myself blushing at all.

But I noticed it. The hon.
gentleman is so accustomed to having to blush for this cause that he does not notice it. I want to know where British Columbia comes in on this. British Columbia has some rights. How they are recognized is difficult to see. Surely out of over $84,000, and producing as we do nearly if not half of the total fish production of Canada-which puts us away ahead of the maritimes, because there is a large fishing industry in Manitoba, which is not generally known-surely we are entitled to a look-in on some of these things.
While I am on my feet and, as the hon. member has introduced it, I would like to revive a twice told tale in connection with an item that appears lower down, "voted by statute," as if that made it any better. That is the question of the perennial wrong done to British Columbia in connection with that item of $160,000 called the bounty, also I suppose for the conservation of the fishing industry. Since I brought this matter up last year and the year before and the year before that, further confirmation has come into my poses-sion which shows that this is not a mere annual fad of mine but that it had engaged the very serious attention of tlhe British Columbia and the dominion governments years ago, and I think possibly also the home government. Here is an item from a British Columbia paper, one of those items carried under the heading, Fifty Years Ago To-day:
The dominion government has received a claim from the government of British Columbia demanding-
I note the word.
-a share of the Halifax fishery award, on the ground that the presence of American fishermen in their waters has seriously interfered with the privileges of their own fishermen. Nothing can be done in the matter until parliament sits, as no allotment whatever has been made to the provinces, individually, and it is not probable that the claim of British Columbia will be recognized, the proceeds of the award having gone into the consolidated funds of the dominion.
That has a double significance. It shows first that British Columbia at that time made a demand, and secondly, it corroborates my statement that that sum awarded under the

Halifax award went into the consolidated fund where it was certainly lost sight of. While I do not propose to burden the committee with the whole brief I might just quote one or two sentences. At that time, 1884, fifty years ago, the question was raised. British Columbia closed its brief to the committee of the privy council thus:
The committee advise that this minute be approved and that a copy thereof be forwarded to the hon. the Secretary of State for Canada, in order that the claim of this province to share in the annual appropriation of $156,000 may be considered by the dominion government, and in order, also, that due consideration may be given to the uncertain and unsatisfactory position of the fishery interests of British Columbia as regards the future.
There was as I say a brief setting out at great length the claim of British Columbia to share in the award. I am not dealing so much with that aspect except as a basis for my claim that we should share in this $160,000 that is being spent now.
Here is another quotation:
It remains only to be added, what is well known, namely, that the fisheries of British Columbia . . . are the richest in the world.
And they deal with that and with other conditions, the inshore fishing grounds, the mild winters and so on, and say there would be a big fleet in British Columbia waters if they got a fair share of this amount. They claim that their statement is a fair and temperate exposition. I also would try to make a fair and temperate exposition. They say that any one with any fairness will recognize the justice of the claim, the grievous injury sustained and so on. Then the brief proceeds:
While highly appreciating the consideration usually given by the government of the dominion to British Columbia matters, so far as they are known to them, yet, as this province is unrepresented in the dominion cabinet . . .
So this province was unrepresented in the dominion cabinet when this deal went through. Then further on:
The Canadian government attribute their unwillingness, in part, to their opinion as to the intention of the Canadian parliament, evidenced by the discussions therein when the grants were made to other provinces without including British Columbia, but it may be remarked that the claim of this province was not then, and has not since been, submitted to parliament in such a manner as to be fully understood-a fact that must weaken materially any inferential argument from the presumed intention of parliament.
That word "inference" is one beloved by the Minister of Finance and also my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. MARCH 13, 1934
Supply-Fisheries-C onservation
Duff) who always says it was inferred that we should suffer this wrong. Then:
Approved report of the honourable the privy council of Canada, 30th April, 1875.
W hich supports this contention, and another one dated December 10, 1879: Then the brief
goes on:
Taking a general view of the matter as it now stands, it is not denied that British Columbia has suffered grievous, exceptional injury by the operation of a treaty not submitted for assent to her legislature, and under which Canada has received a very large sum of money. In seeking redress, the question, practically seems to be whether the provincial claim is to be judged simply by a strict legal construction of the terms and wording of a treaty which it is admitted does not embody the requirements of the contracting parties as expressed in the preliminary correspondence and' instructions, and by a construction which is one of several different interpretations given by competent authorities, and is at variance with the former opinions.
They quote the two minutes of the privy council that I have mentioned, and they go on to say:
Under these circumstances, if the Canadian government do not see their way to recommend a favourable consideration of the provincial claim to His Excellency the Governor General, the. committee advise that they be requested to facilitate a joint reference to the home government . . .
Further:
A very strong feeling exists in the province on this subject, which will be increased by delay in making an adjustment or by the refusal of equitable treatment.
That was in 1884, fifty years ago, so we may judge what the feeling is now in connection with the long delayed justice in this matter:
F or this reason, the committee, in again referring to the matter, express the hopes that the dominion government will review the considerations that have been urged to show the grievances of which British Columbia complains. and the justness of her claim to participate in money received from the home government by Canada, under the treaty which has operated so injuriously to British Columbia.
Then again they repeat their demand that, failing justice, they should be allowed to go to the foot of the throne so to speak. I do not know what the outcome was. There seems to have been a hitch there. As far as I know they did not take it to the home government. If they did the matter was ignored. I am only quoting that as a basis for the demand that I now present. I am not asking that we should share in that $4,500,000 or whatever it was, but I cite it as proof that the best men they had in public life in British Columbia at that time
were strongly of that opinion, and said that there was a growing, bitter feeling against the injustice. But I noticed in the first quotations I read a reference to the money having disappeared into the consolidated fund and therefore could not be obtained. That bears out what I have argued here again and again. The matter will not down until we get justice for British Columbia. This money was put into the consolidated revenue fund and was never heard of or seen again. It could not be; you might as well put a can of condensed milk into the ocean and then seek to recover it. Once anything goes into the consolidated revenue fund it ceases to be ear-marked. These things are common knowledge to all of us. Then some three or four years later, on the eve of an election, the government suddenly decided to spend
8150,000	a year on fisheries bounties, later increasing it to 8160,000, by an act which I have quoted in this house in previous years and which I challenge anyone to quote in contradiction of what I have said. That act never mentioned the Halifax award; it never inferred it or hinted at it in any way. The government simply said they were going to spend so many thousand dollars for the development of deep sea fisheries, and they did so; that is all. Every year we are told that something was left out; that technically I am right but that it was intended to be a quid pro quo for the losses sustained under this award, and so on. That is not so, but even if it were, according to the brief from which I have quoted British Columbia had the same rights. But it is not so, there is no reference to it in the act. I was once in court, and I heard a lawyer who was also a member of parliament trying to argue as to the meaning of an act. He said, "My lord, I was present when that act was put through; the understanding to which we all agreed was that it meant so and so." But the judge said, "I am sorry, but unfortunately they neglected to bind you up with the statute, and your recollection as to what took place does not bind me. I am here to administer the law as I find it," and that is all I am here to ask.
I forget the number of that act, because it is a year or two since I have referred to it, but it is well known and it states that $160,000 shall be spent yearly to benefit the deep sea fisheries of Canada. If British Columbia is not in Canada it is time we knew it. I have brought up this matter on other occasions, and hon. gentlemen just try to pass it off by saying that technically I am right but that the intention was so and so. I do not know anything about the intention; J know what

the act says, and I demand justice for British Columbia.
I am only referring to this item as another illustration of the raw deal British Columbia gets. We are asked to vote $85,000; under this item last year we spent $84,766.31, and I think we got the 31 cents out of it. Is that fair? Can hon. gentlemen expect this sort of thing to promote the harmony and bonne entente we hear so much about? They were able to put through these measures because of their majority; these things took place when British Columbia was not represented in the cabinet and had only two or three members in the house. Times are changing however; even nature is on our side. The population of British Columbia is growing while the population of Nova Scotia is becoming less. At every redistribution we see the representation from Nova Scotia become smaller while the representation from British Columbia increases, so even nature is protesting against the injustice of this thing. The day will come when we will be of greater importance in relation to our numerical strength in this bouse than is the case today, and then we will get justice. I only hope I will live long enough to see that day.	_
Before sitting down I should like to ask the minister what this subsidy is in connection with the ss. Petite.

I am sure we were all interested in hearing the hon. member for Comox-Albemi dwell upon the beautiful scenery in British Columbia and the reasons why, in his opinion, they do not get as much money as they should get. I have no objection to that, but let us look at the situation. We vote $1,443,000 for the fisheries of the Dominion of Canada. I made some hurried calculations while listening to my hon. friend, and I find that of this total $737,543 is spent in British Columbia.
Now let me go a little further. The hon. gentleman speaks of $62 being spent in Canso, and he goes on to say that he does not know where Canso is. I would suggest that the hon. gentleman study the geography of Canada; he is a member of parliament, and he should be acquainted with all parts of the country. I can tell him where Albemi is; I can even tell him where Comox is. I can even go so far as to tell him where the Queen Charlotte islands are, but my hon friend is selfish, and that is not usual in a Scotsman. I am sorry to see that a Scotsman, with such a name as that borne by my hon. friend, should be selfish in the matter of the expenditure of a few dollars.
'Mr. Neill.]
He wants all the money for his own province; in fact I think my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi would like to see this $1,443,050 spent in his own constituency, but that is not possible.
Let us see what is spent in British Columbia. Here we have an item of $25,000 to provide for an investigation into the life history of the Pacific halibut by an international fisheries commission appointed under the Pacific Halibut treaty of March 2, 1923. That is quite a large amount, and it is all for British Columbia; there is nothing for Ontario, Quebec or the little province of Nova 8cotia, which my hon. friend deliberately picked out this afternoon to find fault with because $62 was spent in Canso. Here we have $25,000 devoted to the halibut in British Columbia, and we do not object to that. In fact perhaps I can claim some credit for arranging that this amount should be spent, because it was recommended by the commission of 1922, of which I had the honour to be chairman and of which my hon. friend was a member, that a commission should be set up to protect the halibut industry.
But let me go a little further. Here is an amount of $240,000 for fish culture, and practically the entire amount is spent in the province of British Columbia. If my hon. friend does not get his proportion of that vote it is not my fault. Surely it is not fair for him to rise in his place and try to tell this committee and the public that British Columbia is not getting a fair proportion of the expenditures made by the fisheries department or the government of this country. I hold no brief for this government or for the department; right now I should like to move a resolution that this amount of $1,443,050 be reduced to $1.

The
hon. gentleman is not discussing the correct item; we are discussing item 154, to assist in the conservation and development of the deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $85,000.
I am answering my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni.

I rise to a point of order.
The hon. gentleman does not even know the name of my constituency. It is Comox, but he is pronouncing it " Comax."

After listening to my hon.
friend I knew there was some ox in it. Then my hon. friend interjected into this argument the matter of the Halifax award. Of course this is a hardy annual with him; every year

he gets up and tries to impress upon this house the fact that British Columbia should get part of that $160,000, which is the interest on $4,000,000-
Is it? I do not know.

It is not my fault if you
do not know; why don't you find out? I say, sir, that the hon. gentleman gets up in this committee every year and tries to make out that the province of British Columbia should get a portion of the $160,000, which is 4 per cent on $4,000,000, that was paid by the government of the United States in return for certain privileges on the Atlantic coast. British Columbia had nothing to do with this, but my hon. friend tries to make out that because in the legislation which was brought down the word " Canada " was used instead of the words " maritime provinces," British Columbia should get some of this money. My hon. friend, being a Scotsman, is trying to take part of this money from the maritime provinces. I say to him that British Columbia has no right at all to this money; it is purely a matter between the government of Canada on behalf of the maritime provinces and the government of the United States. British Columbia has never received one cent of this money, nor will she ever receive a cent of it. My hon. friend had better realize that now, because we will never pay British Columbia one cent of this $160,000 a year.
They have no right to it.

Of course not. Let us get
back to the item under consideration. Before doing so may I apologize to you, Mr. Chairman, for having to be called to order. The item now under consideration is to assist in the conservation and development of the deep-sea fisheries, and the demand for fish. To me this seems to be a double barrelled item. First it speaks of assisting in the conservation, which means the curtailment of fishing operations, and then it speaks of a development of the deep-sea fisheries, which means an increase.

My hon. friend seems to
have a pick on British Columbia. I would ask him, please, to forget British Columbia and to look after his Atlantic sea coast.

I am very glad the hon.
member for Vancouver North has made a statement; I can only reply that it was not my fault. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni started this discussion, and that is the reason I have spoken. I am not against British Columbia; my hon. friend should
know that in 1922 I went out to that province for ten weeks, at my own expense, in order to try to do something for the fisheries of British Columbia. I should like to know this from the minister: How does he propose to spend this $85,000, which is voted, at least partially, to assist in the conservation of fish? He is going to assist in preventing people from catching fish, just the same as under the wheat agreement, about which the Prime Minister spoke this afternoon, he is to prevent people from growing wheat. It would seem to me that the expression "assist in the conservation" would mean that the fishermen are not to be allowed to catch fish. Then in the second place, the fisheries are to be developed. How can those two operations work together? How does the minister justify this item? I state he cannot justify it, but I should like to know how he proposes to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I suppose the hon.
member knows that the conservation of fishing means the saving of the fishing industry. The aim of the department is to protect as much as possible fisheries in all parts of Canada and, further, to help the industry. We have to protect fisheries by means of regulations, a course which has been followed for years. That is the way we have protected our fisheries. If my hon. friend wishes, I could give the details concerning the proposed expenditure of this $85,000. Does my hon. friend wish that that should be done?
Yes.

I am surprised at the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough rising to attack the province of British Columbia. I just happened to consult the report showing fisheries expenditures, and I find the figures show that since 1867, the year of confederation, approximately 815,000,000 has been spent on the eastern coast and only 813,000,000 on the Pacific.
We did not attack British Columbia.

But, looking at the revenues I find that almost 83,000,000 has been returned from British Columbia, and not quite $1,000,000 from the eastern provinces.
Mr. MAGDOUGAiDL: Would the hon. member permit a question? How much did this government have to advance to the province of British Columbia during the last three years to keep it from going bankrupt?
What about the Duncan report?
That has not anything to do with it.

We are dealing particularly with fisheries, and I believe an answer is not necessary. The answer to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough is that there are probably more crabs raised on the Atlantic coast than there are in British Columbia.
The hon. member is mistaken, there. British Columbia is the coast for crabs, not Nova Scotia.

However, I do not think we should divide Canada into two parts, the east coast and the west coast. I believe if British Columbia is getting any help she is getting only that which has been long delayed. I am sorry to have to oppose the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough.

Discussion on this item has gone far afield. May I point out to hon. members from British Columbia that while we from the maritime provinces are defending our rights we are not attacking British Columbia.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni did it.

The hon. member for
Comox-Alberni made the suggestion that we were getting that which did not belong to us. I believe we have a perfect right to point out that such is not the case. So far as I am concerned British Columbia can get all the kudos possible out of the fishing busi-

ness. Let me point out however that since hon. members have spoken about favours conferred upon different parts of the dominion, under the agreement between New Zealand and Australia and Canada, British Columbia gets a preference on its fish which is not granted to any other part of the dominion. It is a discrimination in favour of sockeye salmon as against what we should get for our canned fish in the maritime provinces. For that reason I do not believe hon. members from British Columbia have any reason to complain if hon. members from the maritime provinces stand up for their rights.
I had intended to put a question to the minister in the French language, but having begun my observations in English I shall endeavour to finish what I have to say in that language. If I understand correctly, the acting Minister of Fisheries has informed us it is the intention of the government in the near future to establish a biological station on the Gaspe coast. The object of this station is to enlighten the younger generation engaged in the fishing business on the conservation, the greater production and the marketing of fish. I understand the station is to be established in the province of Quebec, and that the lessons given will be, no doubt, in the French language. Perhaps I would not be asking too much if I were to suggest to the minister that the benefits to be derived from the biological station on the Gaspe coast should be extended to the south shore of the Baie des Chaleurs to include certain parts of the province of New Brunswick, such as the county of Gloucester and sections of Northumberland, Kent and Restigouche, where a great majority of the fishermen are of French extraction. The large majority of the fishermen are of French extraction and they should receive the benefits of the teaching in French which will be carried on at the Gaspe biological station. I know that at the present time the French boys from Gloucester, Restigouche, Madawaska, Northumberland and Kent have the privilege of attending a short course in fishing which is carried on at Halifax during the winter time. This is all right as far as it goes but it does not meet the situation. It is too far for the boys to go and besides the general course in French at the biological station would prove of more benefit to our French fishing population. I suggest to the minister that he take this matter into consideration with the view of having the facilities of the biological station at Gaspe extended to certain sections of New Brunswick and if necessary to other sections of the maritime provinces.
