speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
When discussing the organization of the fisheries experimental station at Gaspe with the provincial authorities of Quebec, I had this particular point in view. I hoped to have the benefits of this school extend not only to the French fishermen of the province of Quebec but also to the French fishermen on the coast of New Brunswick and the Magdalen Islands as well as those of Nova Scotia if they should desire to avail themselves of the facilities afforded by the school.
I realize that what has been said by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) is quite true. Advertising is very important in increasing the home demand for fish. I was visited by a delegation last year and I told them that if it were at all possible this vote would be increased this year. My hon. friend will realize that in these times it is very difficult to have a vote increased. The home market is the best market and advertising offers the best medium of increasing the home demand. If we could increase the per capita consumption of fish in Canada by ten pounds we would remedy the whole situation. I can promise my hon. friend that if it is possible to make a saving in the expenditure of this 885,000 we will apply the difference to advertising purposes. I cannot promise that the committee will be asked to vote a supplementary item, but any saving will be applied for that purpose.

We are probably wandering a little far afield from the particular item now before the committee, but I think it may be in order at this time to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). There are few hon. members in the house to whom I listen with greater interest and from whom I derive greater benefit than from that hon. member. But he seems to have an obsession on this particular matter of fishing bounties. Year after year he claims that British Columbia should share in this
8160,000	and year after year we have to go to the trouble of explaining everything to him. We give him the findings of the Maclean commission and we go over the history from the time of the establishment of the tribunal before which witnesses were called. The whole thing had reference only to the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec. The finding of the tribunal was that S5,500,000 should be paid. I think
81,000,000 went for grants, $500,000 for expenses and 84,000,000 was placed in consolidated revenue. It was understood by everyone at the time that British Columbia had
absolutely nothing to do with the matter. That province had no more interest in this than had Manitoba or Ontario. The finding of the tribunal had to do with the advantages which the United States had in our fishing grounds over the fishermen of the maritime provinces and the amount awarded was regarded as recompense. A mistake was made in putting this award into the consolidated revenue fund instead of into a trust fund.
But .they did put it in.

Once it was placed in consolidated revenue my hon. friend thinks it is open to anyone from any place in Canada to come in and grab it. Of course, that is something that we cannot tolerate. While we are willing to do anything to assist the fisheries of British Columbia we cannot allow unholy hands to be placed on this S160.000. I do hope that with this explanation we have heard the last of this matter.
No, never.

I am glad that the hon.
member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has brought up the question of the Halifax award because I wanted to refer to it in another connection. I was a little surprised at hearing him repeat the claims which he had made before as to the injustice which he considers has been done to British Columbia in not sharing in this grant. I feel that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) and those other hon. members who have spoken have done a signal service not only to British Columbia but to Canada generally by placing side by side with the statement of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni the real facts with regard to this particular grant. I do not think he should be allowed to get away with the claim which he so characteristically persists in making. Let us remind him again that the treaty of Washington, referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, provided expressely that American fishermen should be allowed certain fishing privileges in Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, not in British Columbia, and that article 23 of that treaty provided that a tribunal should be set up to award damages to Canada caused by reason of the invasion of our maritime waters by these American fishermen.
To Canada.
To Canada, certainly.

Not to the maritimes.

That tribunal was set up and an award was made. Surely the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is not so unfair as to suggest that when the fishermen of the maritime provinces have paid the piper and suffered the damages the whole Dominion of Canada should participate in the award given by the court. I do not believe he is sincere in making that claim. He does make a technical claim because of the fact that this award was placed in consolidated revenue instead of being set aside for the fishermen of the maritime provinces. This difficulty was realized three years later in 1882 at which time a statute was passed providing, first for a grant of $150,000 and then subsequently for one of $160,000 to the fishermen of the maritime provinces. That amount has been paid out ever since in fishing bounties.

There was no reference to
the award in that act.

No, but there was a reference to the award in the debates that took place in the house at the time, showing why this money was being voted. Surely my hon. friend does not suggest that members from the west or from other parts of Canada would sit there and permit money to be voted to the maritime provinces alone unless they were convinced of the justice of it. Because the preamble did not declare, "Whereas this is money of the people of the maritime provinces," that does not alter the fact that it was money belonging to the people of the maritimes, and it was voted to them to compensate them for the damage they sustained in connection with the fisheries. Moreover, you will find it expressly stated in the debates in the house that this was why the
8160,000	was to be voted each year to the fishermen of the maritime provinces. Since my hon. friend has gone into the question, let us remind him that there remains to be paid the interest for three years. That was the subject of a claim before the Maclean commission, reference to which has been made by my hon. friend from Cape Breton South, and that claim was recognized by the commission. They said that it was a fair claim, holding that the money should be paid for the benefit of the maritime fisheries. Interest on interest had rolled up until it amounted to millions, but the Maclean commission in their report expressly recommended that, considering the grounds upon which the award was made, the request that the three years' unpaid interest be appropriated by parliament to be applied to useful purposes in connection with the Atlantic fisheries or fishermen ap-

peared to them to be fair and equitable, and they recommended that the amount be so appropriated and applied. I do not think my hon. friend wants to take away that little ewe lamb we have in the maritime provinces in connection with this vote. Surely he would not expect us to be paid for damages suffered by British Columbia fishermen with respect to some arrangement with the United States regarding the fisheries on the Pacific coast. These are facts, and while I am pointing them out to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni I want him to understand that we agree with him that the fisheries on the Pacific should receive all the encouragement possible. Apparently however the salmon fishery, so far as exports are concerned, has not done too badly, because this year the increased exports amount to some 8800,000 out of a total increase in export trade of $1,300,000. So that while the British Columbia fisheries are in difficulties they are nevertheless showing some measure of progress.
I come back to the item under consideration. I wish to refer the minister to two or three matters in the maritime provinces in connection with the fishing industry. The first thing I want to discuss is the question mentioned by the hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis, namely, the desirability of increasing demand. One of the objects for which this vote is intended is to promote the demand for fish. Everyone recognizes the good work done by Mrs. Spencer and those engaged teaching the ladies how to cook fish. But after all most of us feel that this does not account for a large proportion of the consumption of what is produced by the industry as a whole. Our export markets have to be taken into consideration. We are all for increasing the home market as much as possible. I am for it as much as anyone else, and I am of the impression that what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis has suggested is a good thing. The minister would be well advised to consider favourably what has been submitted to him in regard to the need for assisting the fishing industry through the medium of advertising. I do not attempt to suggest to him how much money should be voted but I do think that a definite campaign should be undertaken in Canada in the direction of instructing the people in the food value of fish. This is one of the primary industries of the country; it employs a large number of people who use a good deal of gear. A definite campaign along this line would therefore be productive of very desirable results and would increase the national prosperity

substantially. I would ask the minister to assist in the marketing of fish by increasing the demand through advertising. The united maritime fishermen met last November and passed a resolution which I suppose the minister has received, urging upon the hon. gentleman the need for extending assistance along that line. I believe it could well engage his attention, and I submit that part of this money should be used for that purpose. The minister will say no doubt, "We have not enough money." Well, I say to him, use part of the money from the Halifax award still remaining unpaid; it has not yet been paid the fishermen in the maritime provinces. There is one object to which it could be devoted. Remember this-and I am not talking east and west-that we have not had any bonus on the production of fish. There was a wheat bonus two years ago, but we have not asked the government to undertake the stabilization of the fishing industry as it undertook to do in connection with wheat in the west. The Prime Minister made an announcement to-day with regard to the stabilization of the wheat market. We have not had anything of that sort, but we do submit that something should be done to extend the market for fish by stimulating the demand for that product, so as to meet a call which is coming generally from the fishing industry for assistance, not by way of the dole, but by helping men to help themselves. That is all they ask.
There is one other matter 1 wish to mention along lines in which the department might render assistance. I refer to the collection services. The minister has mentioned the collection service for which part of this vote is intended. Everyone naturally thinks of his own constituency, and I have in mind particularly a collection service that could be instituted along the coast between Yarmouth and Shelburne for the purpose of collecting fish -and lobsters by the way-and bringing them to Yarmouth to be shipped by boat to Boston. I would ask the minister to take into consideration the inauguration of services along Clarkjs Harbour, The Pubnicos, Wedgeport and Yarmouth, for the purpose of assisting in the expeditious marketing of the fish produced in that part of the country.
The next matter I wish to discuss briefly is this. I know that the minister and the department have had reports regarding the very serious effect of the storms of last winter on the fishing industry. I do not think that any industry has been so hard hit as those engaged
in fishing. The fishermen have taken a terrific beating; they have lost boats and gear and, most tragic of all, lives. I believe the loss of lives in the fishing industry was something like six.
Seven.

Seven, in the southern and western part of the province of Nova Scotia. Now, I am not discussing a general policy of loans to fishermen, but I did bring to the attention of the minister the circumstances of one fisherman who, through no fault of his own, lost his boat as a result of the storm. It was a total wreck. He has no capital to get another, and he is a good fisherman. He has done well. I should like to find out whether there is not some way in which he can be assisted. As I say, I am not suggesting a general policy at this stage; I am not going as far as that. I am pointing out however that the extraordinary situation which presented itself along the coast this winter ustifies an extraordinary emergency provision for that type of case

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any suggestions to offer?

Yes; there is no question as to what can be voted for assistance to the industry and I think my hon. friend should have an investigation made by his officers and lay down some rule whereby, in emergent conditions, where a man has completely lost his capital, the only thing with which he can earn his living, he may be helped by either a loan or a grant.
Can that not be done under the Relief Act?
Certainly, but the minister was asking me for some general principles to lay down in regard to the matter.
That is the general principle which should be laid down.

There is no doubt that it could be done under the Relief Act. This is an emergency year; the hard winter has created hardships, financial difficulty and distress to the fishermen, and they are asking not for the dole but for an opportunity to help themselves. There again I say that if the minister needs justification for asking his colleagues for more money, it can be found in the Maclean report which points out that the sum of S480.000, without counting interest, is payable still in respect of the Halifax award.
Last year I brought up the matter of the

lobster industry. It has been represented to me repeatedly that the department might do well to consider paying the fishermen for the fantail or mother lobster, that is the large one, which although not showing any eggs, is a productive lobster, which may not be very much good for food, but which at the same time substantially increases the production if thrown back into the water. speechtext: As to the last query of my hon. friend I may say that our latest information is that the bill to which he refers has not yet gone to committee.

I want to thank the minister for information I received from the department with regard to the lobster code, which was giving some concern to the fishermen of Nova Scotia. As the minister knows, a minimum size limit was introduced which was slightly different from ours, but ours has now been made to conform. A maximum size limit was also proposed to be inserted, but later I understand that was struck out. I am sure the lobster fishermen received that news with considerable satisfaction.

I have not time
now to deal with the fishing industry in Nova Scotia, but I intend to do so at a later date. I just want to ask the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth to tell me, when I subsequently deal with the fishing industry of my province, whether he will join with me as a member of the House of Commons, forgetting politics altogether, in assisting the fishermen by helping to bring about the abolition of beam trawlers in Nova Scotia.

I was a member of a
government which passed an order in council which was held subsequently to be ultra vires, but if I had been in the government when that situation occurred, I would have made that order in council effective by having it validated.

All I can say to
my hon. friend is that I am very glad to have his cooperation in that matter.

Under this vote which
mentions conservation and which deals with the regulation of the lobster fishing industry, I should like to ask the minister whether new regulations have been adopted in the county of Prince where there are late and early lobster fishing seasons, and whether, if those regulations have been adopted, they have been properly advertised in the province in order that the fishermen may be made aware of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
No special regulation
was adopted for Prince county, but there was one to limit the number of licences to different districts and this regulation has been advertised as much as possible.

I do not think it has
been advertised as it should. In all fairness to the fishermen and the packers, if the department makes a change in regulations in connection with any section of the country where lobster fishing is carried on, widespread information to that effect should be given. I do not think it would cost the department very' much to insert an advertisement in the papers telling the fishermen that those in a certain section will be allowed to fish only in that section and that only one fishing licence will be issued to each fisherman for the year. The trouble is that I am flooded with letters from fishermen in that locality asking whether this regulation has been put into effect and complaining that they cannot get the information. It should not cost the department very much to insert in the four newspapers in the province a notice telling the fishermen just what has happened. The fishermen migrate from one side of the province to the other. At this season of the year it is often the case, not only in Prince county but in every section, that the lobster packers make advances to the fishermen. This is the season of the year when the fisherman comes in for an advance. He is looking for it in order to equip himself to fish in a certain section. If the packer advances him money to equip himself with gear and so forth and then finds out later that the fisherman is not allowed to fish in a certain section, this is not fair to the packer or to the fisherman. I suggest frankly and in all fairness to the department and the minister that they should advertise in the local papers in that section of the country stating definitely what the regulations are for the coming season, so that the fishermen and the packers may be made aware of the correct situation.

Supply-Fisheries-Conservation

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That regulation was
published in the Canada Gazette, and printed and circulated among the fishermen and can-ners by our inspectors in that district. But if my hon. friend states that some people have been complaining that they have had no notice of that change, I have no objection to putting a little notice in the local papers. It may be an advisable thing to do so. I quite understand that all interested parties should be posted as to the regulations.

I wish first to thank the
minister for having placed in the Magdalen islands an instructor in the curing of codfish. This instructor, whose name I think is Merrier, has done a lot of good work, and since he has been there the curing of codfish has been improved. But the cod fishing industry has expanded a good deal in the Magdalen islands in the last few years, and I do not think one instructor is enough. In the first place he is sent to the islands too late in the season and is retired too early in the fall. He should come when the fishing begins in the spring and should stay as late as November, whereas I think he has been going there late in June and is obliged to come back by the beginning of October. It would be a good thing if instead of one instructor the minister would send two or three and let them stay there through the season. There are quite a few fishermen in the Magdalen islands and one instructor cannot go to all the fishing localities, consequently the instruction given is not sufficient. I would therefore ask the minister if it is possible to place at least two instructors on the island, and send them there earlier in the spring and keep them there until later in the fall.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I thank my hon.
friend for his words of commendation for what we have done. As to the suggestion made by him, he knows that we have had to curtail expenses as much as possible during these years, and we are not prepared at present to increase the expenditure. Nevertheless I can assure my hon. friend that I will look into the matter and see if it is possible to do anything to improve the situation.

I see that this vote is for the purpose of increasing the demand for fish. In Manitoba we have a couple of big lakes, lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba, and not so many years ago they were filled with excellent whitefish that I believe brought the highest price on the New York market. In Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg, although
perhaps we are not very great fish eaters, the consumption of fish could well be developed. But there is a very decided demand for salt water fish, white-fleshed fish-
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but this item refers to deep sea fish, and I imagine the hon. member's remarks would be more in order under the next item.

Well, I have just a word to say. Deep sea fish, fish of the white-fleshed variety, are specially desirable from a medical standpoint, being more digestible and less offensive to a delicate organism than red-fleshed and fat fish, such as the white-fish and pickerel and other varieties that we have in Manitoba. So there is a decided demand and a good market for this sea fish. Of course the only way we get it is frozen hard; that cannot be altered, we appreciate that. But we have to pay twenty or twenty-five cents a pound for this frozen fish. I believe that the fishermen on the Atlantic coast get only one or two cents a pound. I have no suggestion as to a cure for that, except that the dominion owns a railway and that railway operates an express service, and it seems to me this railway and these express facilities could be very well put to work transferring this fish in the shortest possible time and with the least expense to the consumer. If some such measures were taken to develop the business, I think a much greater market could be found for deep sea fish in Manitoba.

Concerning this matter of the conservation and development of our deep sea fisheries, might I, perhaps more for the sake, of information than for anything else, draw the attention of the minister to what I understand to be new regulations that are to come into effect in 1935 in connection with the packing of lobsters. At the present time it is not required that all packing establishments be provided with steam for the cleansing of fish and cans and so on. But I understand that in 1935 new regulations to this effect will become effective, applicable to all canneries large or small, and I fear the result will be that a great many small packers will be put out of business. It is not always easy for them to comply with such stringent regulations, which I do not believe are necessary to keep up the quality of our Atlantic coast packed lobsters. I would therefore ask the minister if it would not be possible to consider an extension of time for the coming into force of this act.

Supply-Fisheries-Oyster Culture

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We have been asked for ameliorations in the canneries from year to year. It is true that the regulations requiring steam retorts in canneries, large or small, will come into force in 1935. Of course it is possible to extend the time, and if after we have heard representations from all the interested parties we think it is advisable so to do, we may extend the time for the coming into force of that regulation.

If that requirement comes into effect it will mean giving a monopoly of the lobster industry to a small group of larger packers who can avail themselves of those conditions. The small packer who under present conditions cannot afford to comply with such regulation will be driven out, leaving the business entirely in the hands of a few large concerns, many of them American packers having branches on this side. I believe in the proper canning of our lobsters, but I do not believe it is necessary that such a stringent regulation should be enforced in order to maintain the quality of our canned lobsters. The Canadian lobster has won for itself an excellent reputation on the markets of the world, and so far as I know nothing has been shown to indicate that that quality would be greatly improved by the enforcement of the proposed new regulation. That is my reason for referring the matter to the minister.

On this item, Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise the same objection that I laid before the committee last year. I appreciate what the government are doing and what former governments have done in the matter of oyster culture, but I cannot agree that the regulation as to the size of the oyster is just. I understand how difficult
fMr. Veniot.]
it is to have a general regulation which will apply to all sections of the oyster fishing industry in the maritime provinces; I also understand how difficult it is to adopt regulations that may be parochial, so to speak, but there are considerations that should be taken into account. For instance, consider what is known as the Caraquet oyster in the county of Gloucester. This oyster does not reach the full size of three and a half inches or more as rapidly as the round oyster matures in other parts of the province. In the cultivated bays of Buctouehe, Shediac and Shemogue we find that the spat is deposited in fre^h water at first in order to bring about a more rapid growth, which allows the young oyster to be placed in colder waters sooner than is the case with the Caraquet oysters. In northern New Brunswick there is no cultivation of that kind carried on, and the Caraquet oyster, and St. Simon bay oysters, have to depend entirely upon nature to reach their mature size. It will take the cultivated oyster three or four years to become marketable, whereas in the case of the round oyster in the northern waters it will take a year or two longer. Under the present regulations three and a half inches is the smallest size at which an oyster is allowed to be caught, and this imposes an absolute hardship upon the oyster fishermen of northern New Brunswick.
Last year I asked that this matter be looked into more fully. I do not know whether or not that has been done, but I am sure no harm would be done to marketing of the round oyster from Caraquet bay if the fishermen were permitted to take them at three inches. I would suggest to the minister that he seriously consider reducing the size of the round oyster to three instead of three and a half inches. Very few small oysters are fished in Caraquet bay, because the regulation is very strictly enforced. I think the fishermen obey the law almost to the letter and return any three inch oysters to the waters of Caraquet bay and St. Simon bay. So I would ask the minister to reconsider the decision that has been made, fixing the size of the oyster at three and a half inches instead of three inches, as it was previously.

Oyster culture, $10,000.

When the house rose at
six o'clock we were endeavouring to get information from the minister regarding this vote, and I must confess that I was not altogether satisfied with such information as he had been able to give up to that time. I really think that we should have a full statement of receipts and expenditures in connection with this vote. It will be observed that the vote is for $10,000, and the minister told us that $8,800 had been expended. We

endeavoured to ascertain from him where that money had been spent and we were unable to find out; all he said was that the largest portion of it was spent in Prince county, Prince Edward Island. It might leave a false impression with the committee simply to be told that $8,000 odd was spent there, and for that reason I should like to have ample information with regard to the item. In addition to that, we tried to get some information regarding the receipts that came in from that area and the minister told us that 327 barrels of oysters had been taken off the public areas in the Bideford section. These were sold at $8 a barrel, making a total of $2,616. Then 153 barrels were sold at $2 per barrel, making in the neighbourhood of $2,922. That amount was taken in as receipts for the oysters picked up around that vicinity. Now, if they were able to pick up about 480 barrels of oysters it would seem that these were fairly good producing areas. We must remember that we are not speaking now of cultivated areas; they are altogether a different matter from the areas off which the 480 barrels were taken. The committee will readily understand that in these hard times of depression the fishermen feel that they should have had the opportunity of fishing these oysters, and even of fishing to a larger extent and selling the product for their benefit, as was always done in former years. But some years ago restrictions were imposed and the areas were closed. Since that time the government and the Department of Fisheries have been handling the industry- Whether they are on the right trlack or not, I am not prepared to discuss at this time. If the department have decided that they are going to follow that course, I suppose all that the fishermen in that locality could do is to put up with it, but the fisheries have been looked upon as a right and the question has arisen whether even the government of the province or of the dominion can really prohibit the fishermen in that community from fishing for oysters in tidal waters. I understand that a test case has been started and is in the supreme court of Prince Edward Island at the present time, and I believe the fishermen intend to take it to the highest court in the land to see whether they are correct in their understanding of the situation.
What I want to point out at present is that if the sum of $8,000 was spent there, the government must have received in rent and sale of oysters some $3,000 or $4,000. I would ask the minister what was collected in the way of rentals this year. There are the yearly rentals for the areas and the new

licences that have been taken out. In all fairness to the people of that community, the government should furnish this information in detail, giving the amount of money received from oysters sold, the amount collected for rentals and new leases issued and all the details in connection with the matter. If the minister can give the committee that information now, I shall be glad to have it.

Mr. MadLEAN: I think it is as important as any other subject.

present time, at $1 per acre. We are pursuing the policy adopted by the former government for the improvement of oyster culture on Prince Edward Island; we have done nothing else.
If the minister will permit, I have to take issue with him there, because under the former government there was never any policy of leasing public areas to private individuals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my colleague will permit me to say a word, I think perhaps what the acting minister has in mind is that the policy which now obtains was arrived at by agreement between the former government of Prince Edward Island and the present administration. As far as I am aware it has been earned out with full approval of the present administration of Prince Edward Island. May I say to my hon. friend with regard to the petition he read from the group of fishermen, although I sympathize very sincerely with them in their plight, I regretted the views they expressed, as I do not think they are in accord with their own welfare. My hon. friend knows full well the oyster fishery that was wiped out in that area was because of free fishing; every man who could hire or buy or borrow or steal a rake would go out and help himself. The result was that a magnificent fishery, which was a source of great wealth to the countryside, was practically destroyed, to such an extent that they had to attempt to restore it by bringing in seed oysters from the United States. This resulted in ruin because they brought with them a parasite which gave the final coup de grace to the few remaining oysters in that area. It is only now being built up through the policy which has been arrived at by agreement, I am happy to say, between the provincial administration and the federal Department of Fisheries. If opportunity is given there can be developed in that area a fishery which will yield in wealth many times more than the whole of the fisheries of Prince Edward Island ever yielded in the past. I am speaking of just that one area in Mal-peque bay alone. It has been estimated by those who have made a study of the matter that soil under the sea suitable for oyster cultivation can be capitalized at SI,000 an acre and yield a profitable return. These very men who signed that petition, if they had their wish, just as soon as these fisheries were built up to a certain stage would go out and tear them to pieces, as happened in the past. What will happen under the present system

Supply-Fisheries-Oyster Culture
of private leases, in which preference is given to those who live in the immediate neighbourhood, is that the individual who acquires a lease, having to pay a certain rental to the government for it and operating under government supervision, will endeavour to build up an enterprise which will grow with the years, producing more and more oysters, and in doing so more employment will be afforded for the very men who signed that petition; and instead of their going out for a few months in the year and raking a few oysters, under a proper system of cultivation there will be employment for them twelve months in the year.
I have briefly expressed my view after having given a great deal of study to the matter, because I have always felt that we have never properly utilized and developed the great potential value of our oyster fisheries in Canada. I believe the oysters from that area are the finest in the world. I have always felt great regret, in going to hotels and clubs throughout the country, even at a time when the United States dollar was at a premium as high as fifteen per cent over the Canadian, that we had to eat the American oyster- which I submit is an inferior oyster-because there were not enough Canadian oysters to supply our own demand. Let me say to my hon. friend and to the committee that if they do not subscribe to the point of view that I have just endeavoured to put forward, at least let us give the policy a chance to work out. It will take a few years, and in the meantime no one will suffer. I am convinced that if it is given a chance to operate under the excellent guidance and supervision of the Department. of Fisheries-and I mention in this connection especially the work of Dr. Needier, who, I am glad to know, according to my hon. friend, has done most excellent work-this industry will thrive and prosper to the great benefit not only of Prince Edward Island as a whole but particularly that of the fishermen for whom my hon. friend has spoken this evening.

I appreciate the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), but those of us who have had actual experience all our lives in that area would have to take objection to some of his remarks. In the first place he states that the oyster industry was killed by overfishing. There my hon. friend is absolutely wrong. The oysterfishery is quite different from many other fisheries, for the life of the oyster industry is the annual fishing; the raking of the beds keeps them
clean and in condition to catch the spat, and in that way you get your yearly crop. What did kill the industry there was the importation of oysters-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because it was overfished. They brought these oysters in because the area had been overfished.

Well, no. If the government had been wise-it was under the local government then-the season would have been shortened to restrict overfishing, and imports of oysters from outside would not have been allowed. If the oyster industry gets back in the public areas to a position where the fisherman can make a day's pay, and he is not allowed to overfish, there is nothing in the world that would benefit the industry to the same extent. Members of the house must realize that these areas include thousands and thousands of acres, and it is impossible for the government to clean them by boats, by drags or by rakes. The only possible way in which they can be cleaned is by public fishing, provided that the areas come back sufficiently to allow the fishermen to make a decent wage. There are some sections at present where they can make some profit. The very fact that 4S0 barrels of oysters were picked up right around this area indicates that the public areas are coming back to quite an extent.
My hon. friend says that this policy was adopted by the previous government. May I inform him and those who were not in the house at the time that I took a very great interest in this matter because these fisheries are right in the centre of the county which I have the honour to represent, and, as the Minister of Finance has said, this industry is worth millions of dollars. My aim, and the deputy minister would bear me out if he were allowed to speak, was to bring back those areas for public fishing under the supervision of the Department of Fisheries rather than for private lease. I wish hon. members who represent fishing counties would put themselves in my position; let them realize if they can what it would mean if the banks off the coast of Newfoundland were leased to private individuals. We have seen the fuss they have had in Nova Scotia in connection with trawlers, and that is only a small instance of what happens when the fisheries get out of the hands of the public. We would like to see these areas brought back in the interests of the public fishermen under the direct supervision of the government. I think I have made a reasonable request, and I hope that

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have only a word to say in reply to my hon. friend, and I should like to emphasize what has been said by the Minister of Finance. During the best days of Malpeque bay, in my hon. friend's constituency, they produced over five thousand barrels per year; in 1912, before this policy was adopted, the production had dropped to four hundred barrels per year. The fisheries had practically disappeared through overfishing in that part of the country. May I tell my hon. friend that the views expressed by the Minister of Finance are shared by outstanding citizens, members of the Liberal party, of Prince Edward Island. I should like to put on record the appreciation expressed by an outstanding Liberal of that province, Hon. Walter Lea, leader of the Liberal party in the province of Prince Edward Island. In 1932, Mr. Lea stated:
I may be treading on very dangerous ground to suggest the approval of any method of protection for our oyster industry, but certainly the cultivation of the beds by the federal department is a very wise move and should have the support of every man in this province regardless of his political affiliations or who was responsible for the change that was made.
I think this expression of opinion should be worth something to my hon. friend.

If the minister wants to
introduce politics into this question, which is the last thing in the world I want to do-

You are down to the
bottom of your argument now.

Let me tell my hon. friend that if he would play politics in a matter of this kind in Pictou county I would not stoop to that in my county. If I wanted to make political capital out of this I certainly could do so, but that is not my wish. This matter is too important for that, and I am surprised that any hon. gentleman holding the portfolio of fisheries should even make the suggestion. I agree with what Mr. Lea has said; we all want to see those areas brought back, but if anyone should get credit for what has been done it is my humble self. I worked hard to get the government to take over that area, and it was only after getting the provincial government and federal government in line that we were able to get the dominion government to take action and spend some money. If my hon. friend wants to raise
[Mr. MacLean 1
political considerations let me tell him that the Conservative government of Prince Edward Island took over those areas and destroyed them, worked them out through careless importation of oysters, without giving any consideration at all to the fisheries. That is the situation, if my hon. friend wants to know it.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to bring politics into this discussion at all. The subject is too important for that; it affects too many people. There are thousands of people in that community who are looking forward to the day when something will be done in their behalf in connection with this industry. It gave them a livelihood for a number of years, and you may be sure that they have had very' hard sledding, as the saying is, since this industry was wiped out. So I hope no one will try to inject politics into this matter. Last year I was even accused by some hon. gentleman opposite of arranging those indignation meetings which were held in connection with the leasing of those areas. I want emphatically to deny that statement. I was sorry those meetings were held. I attended them, as did my opponent in the last election, and we did all we could to reconcile the two factions and get them together. That feeling is there, however, and now it is up to my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries to look after this industry. The government have adopted the policy of leasing, which was never contemplated by the Liberal party; I never gave my consent, and never would give it, to this proposal. I am prepared to stand by the public fishermen as against private interests first, last and all the time. So I am going to leave that matter with the Minister of Fisheries, if he wishes to introduce politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Prince is rather ingenious, to say the least; he proceeds to find fault with the acting Minister of Fisheries for introducing politics, and then he immediately says the Conservative party is responsible for annihilating the oyster beds in Malpeque bay. Of course there is nothing political in that remark. As a matter of fact the acting Minister of Fisheries did not bring in politics at all; his reference was made solely with a view to preventing politics being introduced into the discussion. I may say to my hon. friend that, as Minister of Fisheries during the period when this agreement was entered into with the province of Prince Edward Island, as far as I am concerned I am happy to assume my full share of the responsibility. At the same time I want to

Supply-Fisheries-Oyster Culture
pay tribute to the statesmanship and breadth of view of Mr. Lea, who was the Liberal premier of Prince Edward Island at that time. He had the capacity to rise above petty political considerations and keep in mind only the welfare of the industry itself and those who were dependent upon it. I hope my hon. friend will not misunderstand me when I say that in the maritime provinces we have ample subjects upon which to engage in political discussions and disputes, if we so choose. It is a most fertile area. In fact, I sometimes think that if we cannot find a subject for political dispute we will invent one. But may we leave any discussion of this industry, one which is fraught with such great possibilities for Prince Edward Island and other sections of the maritime provinces, outside the realm of political discussion. I can assure my hon. friend, and I believe I may speak for the acting Minister of Fisheries, that there is no desire to make political capital out of the matter, either one way or the other, and so far as I am concerned I will do my best to keep my eyes focused on the welfare of the industry. I hope the hon. member for Prince will take my word for it that that is the attitude of the acting minister and myself, and I venture the hope that the hon. member will cooperate with us for the benefit and common welfare of the industry.

Before the item passes I should like to say a few words. On one point, namely that of the importance of this industry to Prince Edward Island, I must agree with the hon. member for Prince. It is so important that I believe hon. members on this sicfe of the house do not wish to make a political football of the oyster business in Prince Edward Island. It is admitted to-day that the leasing and cultivation of oyster areas in that province has been a decided success, and while there has been some criticism of the acting Minister of Fisheries, I want to say that in my constituency, one in which great interest is taken in oyster farming, the people are loud in their praises of the policy pursued by the Department of Fisheries and the success it is having in the cultivation of oysters and the renewing of the industry. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I shall look into the matter, with pleasure.

It is very important. One of the biggest branches of our fishing industry in New Brunswick is sardine canning. New Brunswick has at Lepreau the largest sardine canning industry in the world. Some years ago it was proposed to construct a dam for hydro electric power development purposes, which would cross certain sections of Passa-maquoddy bay. It was to cross international waters, and the contention was that the construction of the dam would to a very large extent destroy this industry of sardine canning on the Canadian side.
An act was passed by the province of New Brunswick incorporating a company known as the Cooper company for the purpose of constructing such a dam. An act was also passed by the federal government limiting the time within which such work should be constructed, after submission of the plans and specifications to the departments of fisheries, marine and public works for their sanction. They came back to this parliament for an extension of that franchise, which expired, I believe, in 1929, and a committee of this house, after studying the bill, refused to recommend that the extension be granted. Then it was decided that a thorough investigation should be made by the Canadian and United States authorities; although the greatest part of this work was to be in Canadian waters a small section' of the dam would be on the American side. A certain amount of money was voted in order to carry on that investigation, and I understand that the members of the com-

mission representing the Canadian side of the question were the present deputy minister of fisheries, the head of the biological station at St. Andrews, and some other gentleman. Several meetings have been held; this matter has been under consideration for three or four years now, and I understand from what the minister has said that a report has been submitted to both governments. Since we in the province of New Brunswick are deeply interested in this enterprise and in the protection of this branch of our fisheries I think we are entitled to know what is contained in that report. I think we should be told whether the joint commission is favourable to the construction of the dam and whether they have discovered that it will not interfere with the fishing or destroy the feeding grounds of these sardines. There is only one place in Canada, in addition to the bay of Fundy, where sardines are found; I think the other place is the estuary of the Saguenay river, where sardines are found in small quantities. I believe that many of the sardines canned on the American side were caught in Canadian waters, and if this dam is constructed almost entirely on the Canadian side, and if it destroys the Canadian sardine fisheries, it will mean great hardship and loss to those living along the shores of the bay of Fundy and Passamaquoddy bay. I would like the minister to look into the matter and, if possible, table that report.

I should like the minister to use some of this money in following up the investigation into the habits of the pilchard on the Pacific coast. As the deputy minister knows, the pilchard run was a total failure this year; after a good deal of time had been wasted some steps were taken to hunt for them, and they were discovered a long way off shore. So far as I am aware no one knows why they act that way. We do not even know where they spawn, and this new industry is in a very bad way just now. So I think some of this money should be spent on an investigation of their habits, where they come from and where they spawn. Very little money was spent in this last year; the work was stopped because there was not enough money.

To provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council, for a grant to the United Maritime Fishermen, $4,050.

I wonder if, with fear and
trembling, one might ask for some details of this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The fishermen of the maritime provinces and the Magdalen islands have formed themselves into an association known as the United Maritime Fishermen, with the object of enabling them to better their conditions by cooperation and other means. The association is proving to be of assistance in the development of fisheries, and enables the department to consult with officials who represent the fishermen as a body. Through its efforts improvement in handling and the preparing of fish for market can be brought about much more quickly. The association must depend on fees from the members to meet its expenses. Owing to the present depressed condition of the industry, it seems impossible for the association to procure sufficient funds to enable it to function properly. Hence it applied to the department for aid, and $4,500 was provided last year. Only $4,050 was paid to the association, because ten per cent or $450 was retained against the saving of $14,000,000 mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Provision for that amount only, namely $4,050, is made this year.

How many members are there in the association, and how long have they been receiving this grant? I did not just catch what the minister said as to what they do with it. Do they make any return to the government as to how it is spent, or what does the government receive directly or indirectly in return for the expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The government does not have a report from the association, because we make only a grant to aid in the association's work.
The minister does not know how many members belong to it. That is a rather extraordinary statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I did not say that.

And he does not seem to have a very clear idea as to the return the government receives for its money. I should like to know why the aid is confined to the maritime provinces. Are there no fishermen anywhere else who are hard up in these days? Is there no need for union among fishermen elsewhere-British Columbia, for instance? Some of these days I am going to take a week off so that I may go down to the maritime provinces and see how they-
Why don't your fishermen unionize?

Perhaps because they cannot get a grant. I shall go down and observe in their native fastnesses these strange, weird people with their quaint customs, and with their original ideas, one of the most marked of which seems to be that if there is a loose nickel in the Canadian treasury it belongs to the maritime provinces.
That is all rot.

I do protest that. We in British Columbia are struggling for cooperation. Someone has said that cooperation is organized desperation. In British Columbia we had an organization which went into the canning business, which was not government supported and which, owing to bad times, met with disastrous results; they were ruined. Probably if they had had a friendly hand to give $4,500, even if ten per cent were deducted, they might have weathered the storm. But they were regarded simply as being in business and they had either to sink or swim. My hon. friend talks about not being organized. May I say to him that in British Columbia there are several organizations, and we can very easily give the numbers who belong to them too. We will not have to say that we do not know how

many belong to them. If we can get the guarantee that we in British Columbia, too, will get a share in this grant we will call our association the United British Columbia Fishermen, for the sake of euphony. Would an organization in British Columbia just as good as and for which there is as great necessity as the one now referred to, receive a share of this grant if they make application for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I will tell the hon.
member for Comox-Alberni that this government is as keen to help the fishing industry in the west as it is to help that in the east. If any organization of the same kind had applied for a similar grant I should have been pleased to consider inserting an item in the estimates of my department.
That is very gratifying.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We do not know of any similar organization on the western coast which has applied for any such grant.

I think I can undertake to
say we will have six organizations applying.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend will have all next year to ask for the grant.

To-day is ours; next year is a long time off. We would like a share of this grant. Apart from the remarks I have just made, there is another angle to the matter, namely that of giving some assistance towards organization. The other day I suggested that the fishing industry of British Cdlumbia should get together under some arrangement such as that which the Americans call Nira. That would solve a great many of the problems from which we are suffering. Of course we know that almost the first necessity would be to have the fishermen properly organized. When industries in the United States come under Nira the first action is to encourage workmen to form unions, because that is the most convenient way in which to deal with them, and the workmen can then take their part in negotiating what the code shall be as regards hours, wages and so on. The same could apply to British Columbia. The first essential would be to have some definite form of organization among the fishermen, and a comparatively small grant of a couple of thousand dollars would go a long way towards helping the establishment of an organization along proper lines. Probably as a result of the price investigating committee we may have some form of organization equivalent to the Nira of the United States.

The fishing industry might be glad to take advantage of it, and a vote would be useful in getting the fishermen organized in preparation for such an event.

I am not clear yet as to
what kind of organization this is. Is it an organization of working fishermen such as trade union organization? Is it a cooperative organization, or an organization of employers?

It is a cooperative
organization of fishermen.
Nobody knows.

We all know; we know all
about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The information the
department has is that it is an organization of fishermen operating under a provincial statute for the purpose of bettering the conditions of fishermen, in general. It has proved very beneficial to the fishermen of the eastern provinces.

Are they employees of
some fishing companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It is an association
made up of fishermen.

I have no objection to
fishermen getting a grant from the government, if they can get away with it, but I do think this is a poor way of doing business, namely to give grants to organizations who ask for it. I believe the better way would be for the government to say they are giving assistance to organizations of this kind, and then in turn organizations wherever they may form, either in the maritimes or on the Pacific coast, would make application for and receive a fair share of the grant, in a businesslike way. I object to an organization of this bind going to the government and receiving a grant without such application being made public, while similar organizations in other parts of the country do not receive the same assistance.

Because they did
not apply for it.

If the minister is going
to give assistance of this kind I can assure him that I will not oppose it, but I am suggesting that he should let it be known on the Pacific coast that such assistance is being given. The people on the Pacific coast are in just as great need of assistance and are just as worthy as those in the maritime provinces.

Why did they not
apply for it?

Supply-Fisheries-Grants

I cannot understand the attitude taken by the two hon. members who have just spoken. Apparently they object to the small grant being made to this organization of fishermen in New Brunswick, the Magdalen Islands and Nova Scotia. For many years these men were in a terrible plight due to the disorganization of the industry and they organized cooperatively with the idea of finding out what had caused the depression in the industry and to try to better their conditions. If the fishermen of the Pacific coast do not share in this grant, the fishermen of the maritimes should not be deprived of it. The two hon. gentlemen who have spoken seem to be surprised that this grant is being given to the fishermen of the maritimes. It is about the only grant that is made to the maritime provinces. The western provinces and British Columbia share in many grants made by this government. We would not object if a similar grant were made to the western fishermen or to the fishermen of British Columbia, but I submit that no part of this grant should be taken away from the maritime fishermen. If the fishermen of the Pacfiic coast will ask for a grant I have no doubt that the government will give it, but we cannot subscribe to any sharing of this one. There have been beneficial results from the cooperative work done by this organization; conditions have been bettered and we hope that this grant will be continued. These men are taxpayers and they need even more government assistance. Instead of the grant being shared by organizations in other provinces it should be left intact for this organization.
The minister has said that this organization extends from the maritime provinces to the Magdalen Islands. I should like to know how far those islands are from the mainland of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
About one hundred
miles.

This must be a very loose *organization when it is spread across one hundred miles of water, probably often rough water. One must think in rather wide terms of an association which covers areas so remote from each other. The minister cannot tell me how many belong to it, and it seems to me to be rather a loose kind of association.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It is a well organized association. It has a board of directors and holds a convention every year at which the welfare of the fishermen is discussed. As the
hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) has said, this association has proved to be very beneficial to the fishermen in the maritimes.
I am not opposing the vote in itself; I was simply asking for information which I do not seem to be able to get.
Eighty-five per cent of the fishermen in Nova Scotia are in this organization.
In this one organization.

Yes; it is their own organization.
Mr. MaeINNIS:	I do not think the hon.
member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is opposing this vote, and I know I am not. If the government intends to cariy out a policy of this kind, it should make an announcement so that organizations in other parts of the dominion can take advantage of these grants just the same as the fishermen in the maritime provinces. For instance, suppose the goat breeders in British Columbia should obtain a grant from the government, would not the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) object if a similar grant was not provided for the goat breeders in New Brunswick?

We would be the goat.
Mr. MaeINNIS: We are the goat in this case. The best thing the minister could do would be to let us know if other organizations of a similar kind will receive consideration provided they are doing work along the lines of that done by this organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I stated in answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that if a similar organization on the western coast will apply for a grant and it is found that it is doing something for the welfare of the fishermen, the government will give the matter consideration. The government is just as keen to help the fishermen in the west as it is to help those in the east. Up to the present no request has been made for a such grant to any western organization.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I am sure that there are fishermen's organizations on the coast which are doing just as good work, but they did not know of these grants. They were not as close to the government as the maritime fishermen and consequently they have had to carry on without any assistance.

I appreciate that the
fishermen are going through very difficult

times, but I should like to know upon what basis these grants are made. Are they made upon the basis of membership, of locality, or of work done?

Well, that was the
report of the officials. Of course, we had to be guided by the report. Let me read the first one by way of illustration. Out of this vote of $18,000,
the minister told us yesterday that only $1,300 was spent. In view of that, I do not think it was correct to tell me in October last that there was practically no money to do anything with. I applied to have some work done and was told that there was very little money available this year to clear obstructions, and even to have an engineer sent to inspect the stream it was first necessary to get permission from Ottawa. There are two first class engineers in the department. I do not know what they do, but they are good men, and they cannot have much to do if the total amount spent was $1,300. We had $18,000 voted and in October I was informed that very little money was available, and even an engineer could not be sent to inspect the obstruction until he had got permission from Ottawa. Isn't that penny wise and pound foolish? At any rate I protest at being told that there is no money when there is $18,000.

I wish to make a few remarks
with respect to a matter I discussed in the house on Tuesday, February 20. I believe it is so important, not only from the point of view of the fishermen but from the standpoint of the conservation of fish, that I am justified in taking up some of the time of the committee to deal with the remarks made by the minister as well as by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who replied on that occasion. Of course, under the rules of the house I was prohibited at that time from making any statement in reply, but under this item I wish to take the opportunity to reply to some of the statements made then, because I am firmly of the opinion that many of those statements should not pass without criticism. It is true I did not give the minister any warning that I would bring the matter up before the house went into committee of supply, but I noticed that he was well enough prepared for such a move being made because he had on his desk a report from the deputy minister and was able to produce it and therefore give some sort of answer.
As I have said, previously the whole matter affects over two thousand fishermen on the river, and .the dispute between the minister and myself on behalf of the fishermen relates to seines in the area at the mouth of the Fraser river. In that connection I am sorry that the map I have before me cannot appear in Hansard for the information of the committee, because hon. members would then see at a glance just what I was endeavouring to show the house, namely, that the area allotted to seines last year practically constituted a trap in the mouth of the Fraser river. The minister read from the report handed to him by his deputy that pink and sockeye salmon deteriorate quickly in fresh water. We are
74726-93J
agreed that probably they may deteriorate in fresh water, but the area allotted to the seines is not fresh but brackish water, and we should have that point cleared up. The report from the deputy minister states that the Fraser river follows a well defined channel right across the gulf of Georgia. If his statement is correct, and I say it is, it surely bears out the contention that I have been endeavouring to make, namely that the area allotted to the seine boats last year was right in the brackish water, that is the water of the Fraser river where it mixes with the sea water. He speaks in that report of the comparatively small area north of the boundary line; I shall not go into that because there may be something in his contention that the area just north of the boundary line may be well adapted to seines. But from the map which I hold in my hand-and I am sorry I cannot cross the floor to show it to the minister-I could quickly demonstrate to him that the new line allotted last year went right to the mouth of the Fraser river and with the seines operating there practically constituted a trap. It was not in deep water; it was in water half salt and half fresh. It was in the mouth of the Fraser river and as the deputy minister states in his report, the Fraser follows a well defined course clear across the gulf of Georgia. This line is not across the gulf of Georgia, because the gulf is miles further away.
He said also in that report that there was no demand for Fraser pinks since the canning inspection took place. I have to differ with him there. There was no difficulty experienced last year even with the seines operating, because the fishermen who did catch a few pink salmon had no difficulty except at one period when there was such a glut from the seines that the canneries could not handle the quantity of fish landed there in one day, and one fisherman who was offered one and a half cents apiece for his salmon, took them across the line and received four and a half and five cents for the same fish from the canneries on the other side.
Just at this point might I also criticize the inspectors because they bring in a report to the minister which he read into Hansard. It should be seriously noted that the three inspectors are also brokers. I think it is contrary to all business practice that men who are in the brokerage business and themselves buying fish should be inspectors appointed by the government. I do not think any other business would tolerate such a situation. I am not casting any blame upon the inspectors so far as their integrity is concerned, but it is
1466	COMMONS
Supply-Fisheries-Disbursements
not a good principle to allow brokers who are in the business of buying to be also the inspectors who go out and inspect the fish they buy and have a right to condemn or to pass as they see fit. Human nature being what it is, this is a wrong principle. If that is going to be done, there should be at least two outside inspectors as well as the three permanent men who are brokers.
In the report made by the deputy I take strong exception to another statement where he says that the gill netters were not hurt by the seiners. I quoted the figures, and *1 am going to quote them again because I got them authentically from the fishermen themselves. They show that before the seines were allowed to operate the fishermen were getting anything from three hundred to five hundred fish a day, and last fall, after the seines started in the mouth of the gulf, their catches dropped, some getting only five, some ten a day, but not any more than fifty a day were picked up by any of the fishermen in the Fraser river. To substantiate my case further, I have in my hand a report from one of the cannery men who control to a considerable extent gill net fishermen and who have several boats operating from the canneries. The report I received from that cannery is that last year when the seines operated, they were picking up only two hundred to three hundred fish in an area as against seventeen hundred the year previously. The statement made by the deputy minister that the operation of seine boats in the mouth of the Fraser river has not hurt the fishermen, I say is not correct; it is not a statement of fact, because I am quoting the figures as given to me after a careful scrutiny and study of the situation right on the ground last fall.
I should like to ask the minister a question and to have him take serious note of it. Has he any figures showing the number of fish caught after September 14? Whether fish are caught out in the gulf or in the mouth of the Fraser river or up the Fraser, it is well known to us who have made a study of the matter that the fish begin to deteriorate after a certain date, and many of the can,nary men refuse to can fish caught after September 17. Even on September 14 it was noticed that the fish had begun to deteriorate a little. I wonder whether the minister has any record regarding fish canned or caught after September 14.
As regards the quantity of fish that was condemned, I do not think it is so alarming, and I am going to dispute the minister's statement that last season, out of 524,000 cases of pink salmon packed in British Columbia,

13,000 cases were classified by the inspection board as second quality. I wonder whether the inspection board really inspected 524,000 cases last year. Did those three inspectors go through all those 524,000 cases of salmon for inspection? But even if that were possible and they did so, the number rated as second quality is only about two per cent of the total and there was a leading letter sent out to the canneries asking them if those fish were caught by gill nets or seines. One cannery man stated to me-and I shall not give his name because it might affect him with the other cannery men-that in his opinion this letter from the department was certainly intended as a leading statement to find out if possible whether they could attribute the poorer quality of the fish to the fact that they had been caught by the gill netters after they had entered the Fraser river.
Regarding the board of inspection, their report says:
The ooening of waters off the Fraser to seining would appear to have led to a much improved quality in respect to a large portion of the pack at Fraser river canneries and canneries in the Vancouver area packing so called Fraser river pinks. The individual experience of each member of the board over a long period of years has been that the great bulk of the Fraser pink pack has been of such a character that under the inspection now in force it would have to be classed as second quality for lack of firmness.
I pointed out just a few minutes ago that it all depends on the time or the period the fish are taken out of the water. After September 16 last year I believe they did begin to deteriorate. The matter is not just one of the area in which the fish are picked up. Very often it depends to a large extent not on the area but on the time they are picked up. The minister has accused me of seeing only one side of the picture. That may be quite true; I see one side standing out all the time. In fact I see two; I see the cannery men who control and own the seine boats making an attempt in British Columbia to drive the gill net fishermen away, because if that could be brought about, the canners then would be virtually in a position to control the whole industry. They would own the seine boats going out; the ships and the payment of the crews would be in their hands and they would not have to take any notice of the gill net fishermen. I can. see on the other side over two thousand individual fishermen being driven off the area of the Fraser river and so deprived of their living. I appeal to the minister, because it is a serious matter not only to the fishermen but the point of view of conservation of the fish. It is true that

Supply-Fisheries-Disbursements
under the regulations opportunity is supposed to be given for the fish to go up the river during the week ends. But if the intent of the department is to conserve the fish why allow these seines like birds of prey to devastate schools of salmon? In some instances they are picking up eight to ten thousand fish at one time. If the purpose of the minister or his officials is to deplete the waters of the Fraser river, certainly they went the right way about it by allowing over sixty seine boats to operate in the mouth of that river last year.
Looking over the annual report of the department I notice that the pack of sockeye salmon, if not of all salmon, has been going down. I wonder if the minister has noted that, and if he can tell the reason why, in spite of the operations of the hatcheries and the fact that thousands of dollars are being spent in the effort to maintain the supply of fish artificially, the catch of sockeye salmon has been decreasing since 1925. This year, with the regulations put into force by order in council, if the seine boats are allowed to operate they will also pick up the late fall run of sockeye salmon. Yet we are told that fish must be conserved, and fishing must cease over the week end to allow a certain number of fish to escape. But there will be no escape if these seines are allowed to operate; with large nets picking up eight or ten thousand fish at a time we will very soon have no fish at all coming into the Fraser river.
Then the minister might tell the committee why the twenty-four hour rule was changed this year. When the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and myself protested last year against this order in council, the acting Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us at considerable length why it was necessary to put that twenty-four hour regulation into effect. But this year without a word they have cut it out. It will be interesting to hear why it has been cut out. It shows that we were right and that the whole matter should have been put before the marine and fisheries committee. I do not know how many changes have been made in the Fisheries Act since it was passed by this house; there must be dozens-
More than that.

Yet we have the marine and
fisheries committee with nothing to do, while everything goes through by order in council, although the lives of hundreds or thousands of fishermen are affected. All these things should have been referred to that committee.
I would like to know why they were not, why the committee should not have a chance to deliberate on them. I would remind the minister that this is the only place where the fishermen have an opportunity to air their grievances. They cannot afford, like the canners, to send men to Ottawa to lobby on their behalf; they have to depend on the members of parliament to state their difficulties in the House of Commons. If these matters had been referred to the committee where we could have gone into them and called the officials of the department and asked them the why and wherefore of things and taken the time to see that all interests were being protected, it would have been far better for the industry as a whole.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke of the sockeye salmon treaty. I wonder if the minister has any information as to the possibility of that treaty passing in t'he United States. I was rather surprised that the minister mentioned that, because if my information is correct it is a pity it was not passed when it was first introduced in this house; the opposition which resulted in its delay for a year was, I believe, the cause of the United States not accepting it. In 1929 Mr. Tolmie, then premier of British Columbia, and his cabinet, agreed that the sockeye salmon treaty was one of the best things put forward on behalf of the fishing industry, but it was delayed here for a year. I am not sure whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce objected, but I know many hon. members on that side did, and the fact of the treaty not being passed in the United States was due to the opposition it met with here in 1929 and 1930.
I would also draw the minister's attention to some of the figures that have been quoted by the deputy minister in his report. They do not exactly correspond with the figures in the annual report. I find that for 1929-30 the report speaks of 158,290 cases, but in the inspector's report to the minister the figure is 161.529. In 1931 the inspector's report states that there were 20,000 but the annual report says 21,534. When they are giving figures to the minister they should see that they correspond with the official figures given by the department. I have spent some time looking them up and have endeavoured to quote them as correctly as I can from the information at hand.
I am earnestly appealing to the minister not to allow seines to operate in the mouth of the Fraser river. I appeal to him again to let the matter go before the marine and fisheries com-
