mittee so that it can be dealt with there and maps and data produced, with the fishermen present. Surely that is not asking -too much, especially when, as I have stated, it affects the living of over two thousand fishermen. If the greatest good for the greatest number is the object, then the policy of keeping seines out of the mouth of the Fraser river should be followed. Permit them, if you 'like, in the small area next to the international boundary, but do not allow them in the waters of the Fraser river or anyway near the entrance to that river. I would like to have the minister answer some of the statements I have made.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
With respect to the
question of purse seining and gill net fishing, I cannot add anything to what I said to the house some -time ago when I put on the record the statement of the officials of -the department. As minister I have to rely of course on the reports of our officials. The contention of my hon. friend may be right or it may be wrong, but we have to rely on the reports of our officials. According to the information received from those in the industry in general in the west, they are competent men and their reports as a rule are accurate.
As to the twenty-four hour regulation, my hon. friend say-s he opposed that regulation last year and; wants to know why it was repealed this year. The aim of the department was to prevent fish in bad condition being canned, and as some men were carrying fish a long way before it reached the canneries we tried the regulation with that object in view. It worked pretty well up until last	August. I	told	the house	lastyear that it was only a trial we were making. From August to the end of the fishing season we did not have officials in sufficient number to ensure	the proper	enforcement of	thisregulation,	and that is the	reason it	was
repealed. Furthermore, it was not necessary at the end of the season.
As to the inspectors my hon. friend was complaining about, he says it is a wrong principle that brokers should1 be appointed inspectors. I desire to say that these inspectors were recommended by the canners who were	interested.	We	never had	any
complaints about their work.
In addition my hon. friend very strongly urges that these questions of regulation and so on should be referred to the fisheries committee. I have no objection to that principle, and I can tell my hon. friend that when important questions are raised in this house I am prepared to recommend that such questions be referred to the committee.

What is more important than
the question we are now discussing? A commission was appointed in 1922, composed of members of this house some of whom are still here; they went to British Columbia and investigated conditions, and in their report they recommended that if at all- possible seines should be done away with entirely. There is no question more important than the one we are discussing at the moment, so why will the minister not refer the matter to the committee?
Mr. DURANLiEAU: I shall be pleased to discuss the matter with my colleagues and I will inform my hon. friend whether or not it is thought advisable to refer this question to the committee.

There is a reduction of
$130,000 in this item. If the minister and the government are trying to do something for the fisheries I should like to know how they can afford to reduce this item by that large amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
remember that in his budget speech last year the Minister of Finance promised that a further cut of $14,000,000 would be made in the appropriations. In carrying out that promise this reduction has been made. Last year we carried on with satisfaction, and this year we hope to be able to do the same.

I must object when the minister tries to say that this reduction is made because the Minister of Finance asked him to be economical in his department. The Minister of Finance has troubles enough of his own without having the acting Minister of Fisheries try to blame him for a reduction in this vote which has to do with what I -consider to be a natural industry in this country that has the best opportunity for development.
The minister also stated that in spite of this reduction the department had been carrying on satisfactorily. I cannot agree with him in that; in fact if I were not a member of parliament I would put in a bill to the Department of Fisheries for work I performed myself. The minister cannot say that the work of his department in the matter of inspecting fish, for instance, and looking after the fisheries, has been done properly. I am a living example of proof to the contrary, because I had to do the work myself. The minister must know that because of the reduction in this item there were not enough inspectors during 1933 to examine and in-

spect properly the fish which the fishermen had to market. Before I proceed I should like to know whether or not the minister is aware of that fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is no doubt that at times we had some difficulty in having the inspections carried out at the proper times, and our inspectors had to work very hard, but we did our best with the money available.

I do not say that the department did not do its best, but the fact remains that the inspection was not carried out properly. I have personal knowledge of the fact that thousands of barrels of pickled fish lay in the fishermen's sheds and on the wharves of the purchasers for days and weeks before the inspectors could get around to inspect them. Let me tell the minister why that was so. A few years ago we had what were known as overseers as well as inspectors. The department wanted to be smart and to show parliament and the country that they were trying to do something, so they amalgamated those branches and made the overseers inspectors. Nine out of ten of those overseers of fisheries did not know a kyack from an alewife, and I doubt whether the minister knows the difference. However, they amalgamated those two branches and deliberately made inspectors of those overseers, who were good men as overseers and who had been in the department for many years. They dismissed the men who had been inspecting fish for years, and the result has been that -these overseers did not have the qualifications properly to inspect pickled fish, mackerel and herring. The inspection last year was an absolute farce, and the exporters of fish had to suffer for it. Although the stamp of the department was on the barrels, when the fish reached the West Indies and were opened it was found that they were not up to the standard which was stated on the labels. It was not the department, the minister or the deputy who suffered; it was the man who bought the fish and shipped them to the foreign market, and I want to say to the minister that this policy was wrong. There should be special men to inspect fish, entirely apart from the overseers. The minister should go back to the old policy of having overseers do certain work in connection with the fisheries and properly appointed inspectors in the different districts to look after the inspection of fish.
Let me give an instance. In the county in which I live, a county wThich last year must have produced twenty thousand barrels
of pickled fish, there were only two inspectors. In the middle of the season, when there were ten or fifteen thousand barrels of fish to inspect, one of those inspectors resigned, and what did the department do? They appointed a hotelkeeper, not as an inspector but in order to get around the law. The department would not ask the civil service commission to call for applications for a properly qualified inspector, but the minister appointed a fishery guardian to take the place of the fish inspector. This particular fishery guardian, a personal friend of mine and a hotelkeeper, was appointed in place of a man who should have been the fish inspector. Of course a Tory government was in power, and they have a right to appoint their own friends; I am not complaining about that. I do want to say to the minister, however, that in the middle of the fishing season, when there were fish to be inspected, they allowed the retirement of the regular inspector and instead of calling for applications or appointing a temporary inspector who would know a codfish from a haddock, the minister appointed as fishery guardian a man who had practically never seen a codfish, except on his hotel dining room table. Why was that done?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Does the hon. member refer to Evans?
I am referring to the retirement of Mr. Evans.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am informed he
was not an inspector who inspected pickled fish; he was not qualified to do that, and never did qualify.
Surely that is not an answer to my complaint. Mr. Evans was an official of the department for twenty-five years. During that time he certainly inspected fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Not according to my information; he was an inspector, grade 1, and was not required to inspect fish.

Grade 1 is certainly the
highest grade in inspectorship.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is the lowest.

Mr. Evans certainly inspected
fish, because I have seen him doing it with my own eyes and to my own knowledge. I have been there at the time. Anyone who says Mr. Evans did not inspect fish does not know what he is talking about. But even if he did not inspect fish why did the min-
Supply-Pensions

ister, upon Mr. Evans' retirement, camouflage the situation and instead of appointing a fishery inspector appoint a guardian in order to give one of his friends a job?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That was only a
temporary appointment; we want a grade 2 inspector, and the civil service commission is at the present time filling the position.

I am very glad that at last
my protest has received some notice from the minister. If I remember correctly it was last July I wrote the minister about it, after receiving protests against the appointment by fishermen at Blandford and Mill Cove. I wrote the minister, and received a number of letters from him in which he tried to excuse the department and excuse himself for appointing this hotelkeeper not as a fishery inspector but as a guardian. That was a time when the fishery inspector was needed. Why does the minister only now come along and say that he is going to have this position filled, when it should have been filled last year? I am glad to hear the position is to be filled, but surely there was no reason why this man should have been paid $1,000 per year to act as fishery guardian when men could be got to do the work for $75 a year.

A newspaper report of
the proceedings of the Campbellton board of trade would seem to indicate that definite in-

formation has been received from the minister. This report reads:
A letter from Hon. H. A. Stewart, Minister of Public Works, Ottawa, indicated that an appropriation of $32,000 was being considered for dredging on both sides of the deep water wharf pier, this work to provide a depth of 24 feet at low tide in the several berths on the north side of the wharf and to make the inside berths also usuable by ocean going boats.
It is very important that this work should be done early this year. As I have mentioned already, three ocean going steamers were grounded in this harbour and their cargoes bad to be jettisoned with almost a complete loss to the shippers. I ask the minister to adhere to this amount of 332,000 which he seems to have in mind, or, if possible, increase it so that the channel at the mouth of the Restigouche may be made safe for ocean going steamers. This port should be in such a condition that large shippers of lumber could feel free to invite foreign ships to come in and load. Otherwise, these people will suffer great loss.
I submit that some work should be done at Dalhousie. There is a large and well organized industry at this port, which is the second winter port in the maritimes. Last year it was open for sea going ships until the last day of December. A small expenditure on this port would make it more easily available to ocean going traffic. Incidentally it will help the Canadian National Railways if these ports are able to take care of large ships. We would be able to get much of the traffic which now goes to northern Maine and which is usually taken up by rail. Greater facilities should be provided in order that our railways can secure this heavy traffic of fertilizer, automobiles and potatoes which can be handled with only a one hundred mile rail haul.
